They simply ask that these Bills shall not be reported, because, if they are, the calculations of the province will be upset entirely; it will mean the duplication of their line from Toronto to the international boundary; it will mean the needless expense of millions or tens of millions of dollars. The hydro people will have either to take over the Canadian Northern railway at a greatly enhanced price or to build their own line, and in that case there will be duplication, although, from present appearances I think the hydro line will be built before the Canadian Northern railway line. These Bills have been renewed four or five times; they have been on the statute books inoperative and stale, for thirteen years in one case and for seventeen in the other, and all that is asked is that they be left on the statute books without any further renewal.
Something was said about public ownership and the cost and the impossibility of operating publicly-owned railways at cost. We in Canada are behind some of our neighbours in the states in not having as many radial railways as they have, but we have some publicly-owned lines. In the western and central paTt of Ontario, from which this strong feeling comes, we have in the Guelph street railway a sample of what can be done in publicly-owned and operated street railways. The Guelph street railway was municipalised some years ago, and it now pays a dividend of from 20 to 25 per cent. The railway recently built from London to Port Stanley was jeered at, just as these hydro-radial roads have been, but it was put in operation and in the first six months, before it really got down to business, it showed a net profit_ of $10,000. Therefore, there is no reason to predict that these publicly-owned and operated

railways will be carried on at a loss. There is no reason to doubt the accuracy of the Estimates, and the plans and undertakings made for the ultimate fulfilment of the intention and design of the Hydro-Electric . Commission. They have undertaken everything in a thorough and businesslike way and they can be trusted to' handle this matter in the public interest.
As I say, the Hydro-Electric Commission has reduced the cost of electric power from 100 to 300 per cent, and there is no reason to believe that the operation of this HydroRadial Railway Commission will be any less successful, or will be less a public benefit. I would ask the committee to bear in mind the often-expressed wish of the province of Ontario and the municipalities that are spending their tens of thousands of dollars for the introduction of this system, and to be fair, about it and even generous about it if necessary, and leave the people of Ontario to work out in their own time and by their own methods the successful operation of this hydro-radial system.

It seems to me to be wholly unnecessary to dwell upon the success or otherwise of the Hydro. That matter has been before the public of Ontario, and the success of the system has been endorsed by both parties repeatedly and almost unanimously. Underlying this whole question, of course, is the principle of public ownership. That also has received almost universal public approval. At the present time, as I understand it, the argument is that the Canadian Northern Railway should have an extension of their charter for a certain line. If it were a matter of justice, of absolutely clear justice, whether they should have their charter extended or not, the question of public ownership and the rights of the province of Ontario in the future would not really come in. But such is not the case; it is merely a matter of ordinary, common business advantage. And when the Government of Canada chose to tie itself up, by guarantees or otherwise, to the Canadian Northern Railway, and now find themselves in a tangle over it, they are only trying to excuse one fault by another, and they can not really aggravate the situation by opposing the express wish of the province of Ontario as represented by its Government. I took occasion to ask the Government of Ontario-that is, to ask the Prime Minister -some little time ago if they intended to oppose this Bill. I wanted the fact brought out technically and properly. They said they were instructing and send-

ing their men to that end. If this committee feels that it has a right, for an ordinary business matter, not involving the principle of justice, to oppose the province of Ontario and do a serious injury to the whole principle of their hydro-electric scheme, the very darling of the people of Ontario, and as asserted, to cause very serious loss to the province of Ontario, this committee, and the Government of Canada will have done the province of Ontario a very serious wrong.

Being sponsor on the Order Paper for this Bill, I desire to make a few observations. I would have much preferred to speak later in the debate, but I have been suffering from serious complaints affecting my hearing and my throat, and think it better I should speak to-day. The Bill has been before the Committee on Railways on four or five different occasions. Since I entered Parliament I have never seen any Bill that had so much attention given to it, especially by those opposed to it, as has been given to the two Bills in question. Those who favoured the Bill were hardly, if at all, heard. Under these circumstances the committee voted, by the very considerable majority of two to one, in favour of putting both these Bills through. The opposition to the Bill, as is well known, came from the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario, and one specific argument put forward in the Railway Committee, as here to-day, has been that the matter is one peculiar to the province of Ontario. That view is not a broad one, and I entirely refuse to accede to it and expressly dissent from it. It is , true that the radial roads in question will be provincial, but it is equally true that the Canadian Northern railway system is a national highway affecting not only Ontario but all the provinces of the Dominion. Therefore, I am of the opinion that this question should be dealt with from a broad and national standpoint. In dealing with the argument put forward, that the Ontario Government have sent here a resolution asking the members of this House to oppose these Bills, had I been a member of the Ontario House-a body for which I have every respect-in the light I now have, I would have stood up, even if I had been the only member to do so, and would have voted against [DOT] any such resolution being sent to this Parliament. To yield to that , argument would be to surrender all the cardinal functions of this House; it would
be to acknowledge the principle that, because of a local situation and of a resolution sent from some provincial House, this Parliament should accede to these requests and recede from its position, whether well taken or not. I can not submit to that myself, and I do not propose to. Some of the members from Ontario are quite inconsistent in this regard, especially those on this side of the House.
Talk about the Bill, and not about the members.

Some of the members, I say, are inconsistent-and I am addressing myself to you, Mr. Speaker. I hope that the members who support the commission will not be so arbitrary, or so arrogant that they will not permit a member who takes part in this debate to even mention them- I do not apprehend that it is part of the privilege of members to object to such mention. They say that the principle at stake is one that is provincial, not general. So was the question of free wheat in the West. Yet all these gentlemen who were so glib to-day rushed in to take care of the western farmer upon this question, which is more specific to the western provinces' than this is specific to the province of Ontario. I think the matter of these Canadian Northern Railway Bills is essentially a matter for this House. I equally think that the matter of free wheat was essentially a matter for this House. My view is that members of the Dominion Parliament represent in this House, more than their respective provinces or counties; they represent the whole Dominion. To hold any other view would, in my opinion, be derogatory to the position hon. members hold in this House as representatives of the people of Canada. Hydro-Electric railways are essentially provincial. But the Canadian Pacific, Grand Trunk, Grand Trunk Pacific, Transcontinental, and Canadian Northern railways are Federal railways, for the general advantage of Canada, and upon qutestions affecting all these great roads, I hold, every member has the right to express his opinion from the national point of view, and should do so. The Hydro-Radial Commission and those interested in it knew that these charters existed, and had been renewed, and that the railways proposed to be built under them had been declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. They knew that these charters formed part of the Canadian

Northern railway and were intended as an important feature to that system.
They knew that about $1,800,000 had been invested by the Canadian Northern people in building lines and making surveys and paying for lands for entrance into the city of Hamilton. They knew that bonds were sold to innocent purchasers, and it would be unfair to them if such treatment were handed out to the Canadian Northern people. They knew that this country, through this Parliament, has been committed to a guarantee of $46,000,000' and an advance by way of loan and otherwise of something like $30,000,000; that the provinces of-the West, all of them, I think, have pledged their credit to this great national highway by way of advances or guarantees; that everything that goes from Quebec to the Atlantic in connection with the Canadian Northern railway goes as a national undertaking to which the people of the country are committed. When the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission sends its steam roller down here with flanges on it to scrape everybody off the road, I am impressed by the fact that that steam roller is on the wrong track. I cannot conceive it as fair that hon. gentlemen here should attempt to twist this matter. The real issue is the national idea which is embodied in this great Tailway; the side issue is the provincial element. That latter element seems to be put above the national element by some people, and to overshadow it in all its phases. There is nothing to prevent the Hydro-Electric railway from going on with its work. It has to compete with the Canadian Pacific railway, the National Transcontinental, the Grand Trunk railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Are they afraid of this alleged bankrupt railway, that they cannot compete with it? The confession that this would be a death blow to hydro is the weakest argument that I have ever heard. It seems to he that I am a better champion of hydro than these gentlemen. I do not think that they are living up to the great possibilities of hydro in this country. A national highway of nearly 10,000 miles is surely worthy of consideration; a splendidly built, well-ballasted and well-equipped transcontinental road, a credit to the Dominion, serving the people of the East as well as of the West, handling more than one-third of the wheat crop yearly, having grades unsurpassed by any other Transcontinental road. One engine hauls from Quebec to Vancouver, a train about a quarter of a mile long with fifteen Pullman and 
baggage cars, and the same engine hauls it from Vancouver back over the mountains to Quebec. I think that is very creditable. One of these railways will perhaps be the keystone to the salvation of our country when the whole deplorable railway situation comes to be settled.

Do they think that if
they should not get this extension, it would be a blot on their title if they should want to see out the whole Transcontinental system?

I do not know anything about blots or titles; I have not attempted to argue anything about title. If my hon. friend will be content for a while he will probably see a little later what I am leading to. There are $400,000,000 invested in this great Transcontinental system. A serious situation confronts this country. I do not know that it is well for any member to speak of it, but since it is in my mind I purpose referring to it. A serious situation confronts this Parliament and the country upon the whole railway question. Railway conditions constitute the great problem for the near future of Canada. I ask hon. gentlemen: having assisted the Canadian Northern railway, why injure it? Why attempt to pull it down? Would you extend your left hand to a man in the water, pull him to shore and rescue him from drowning, and then hit him with your right and send him back into the water? It is not the ordinary way of doing business, but that is what hon. gentlemen are doing who voted for the grant of $45,000,000; who committed themselves to grants made by this Parliament. A tidal wave of local conditions and local feeling which they cannot resist causes them. to swallow themselves and swallow their votes. I thought better of the province of Ontario than that it would produce men who would do just that thing. The Hydro-Electric Commission wants subsidies from this Parliament, but they do not want any one else to get any subsidies. The Hydro railway claim was based and founded on the proposition of obtaining Dominion subsidies. Can they come back to this Parliament after the attitude they have taken and ask for subsidies? To my mind, the Hydro Commission has made the most egregious mistake of its existence. I believe that Hydro is greater than its supporters in this House or than the Chairman of the Commission believe it to be. I have al-

ways been a supporter of the Hydro; I have 'looked forward to its glorious possibilities. I believe that hon. gentlemen make a mistake when they come here and say that they are not asking for subsidies from this Parliament; that they do not want subsidies; that they will build the roads themselves. I say that they are making a mistake, because I 'believe that Hydro shouM have the support of this Parliament as a great national undertaking, even though it is provincial. I am prepared to go further than friends of Hydro here in that regard. What are the possibilities of Hydro? Lake Superior, with its thousands of square miles of water, is the basin that sends down through the various waterways and channels to our lower lakes-and to the province of Ontario, where the Ontario Government has caught it-a stream of silver which is being turned into a stream of gold, an asset greater in value than all the minerals which have been taken out of the ground and all the minerals yet in the ground, an asset greater than the fisheries or timbers of our country. Why? Because these last are evanescent and will pass away, but Hydro will last forever. Every drop of water in all these splendid watersheds contributes to this great asset to the people of Ontario, who are making splendid use of it. As they have such a heritage as this, I arm not fearful of the lack of Hydro power to pe able to compete with the Canadian Northern Railway, with the Canadian Pacific Railway, or with any other railway. It is a confession of weakness to suggest any such thing. Its ability to compete is undeniable. They have cut power rates in half, as the hon. member for South Oxford has said; they have cut lighting rates in half. The ability to compete is general, and has been of great benefit to thp people of Ontario. But is is 6aid that they cannot compete at Niagara, right at the centre of power, in that district which is industrially the greatest in Ontario. It is said that the Canadian Northern Railway is taking a little piece of right of way in the most densely populated part of Ontario, a district where the hum of industry is heard; a district that will some day require three or four additional railroads. That district will then furnish a splendid paying business to this great Hydro- Electric railway system, to the Canadian Northern, to the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo, to the Canadian Pacific railway,
and to the Grand Trunk. Unless I am mistaken that development will occur in spite of the heavy drain of the reconstruction period following the war. This charter is not a new charter. These gentlemen have forgotten to tell the House that since the Canadian 'Northern railway took over this charter under Bill No. 8, within the last six years, they have, within the last two years, built 12 miles of railway, and yet they are referred to as paper charter mongers. They have, as has been stated, built 76 miles of road in that particular section of the country. What for? To be links and feeders to their transcontinental system from the Niagara frontier inwards to Toronto, to tap the lake traffic, to better the trade for their own lines, with their own men, under their own management, so that they can give to the West cheaper freight rates, so that they can receive from the steamers on the lower lake system of the province of Ontario freight that comes cheaper by lake, so that they can get in their coal at different points and to the best advantage. This will benefit the whole Canadian Northern railway system which the Government has pledged itself to support.
'They are not shut out.

Who wants somebody
else to run their business? The HydroElectric is a provincial line. What benefit can they be to the Canadian Northern railway that they cannot be to the Canadian Pacific railway? If they object to the Canadian Northern railway, why should they not object to the Canadian Pacific railway running? Is it the case that every charter that is going to be asked for is going to be condemned because the HydroElectric Commission want to take that particular right of way?
Hear, hear.

I trow not. I hope we have not yet got to that situation in the Dominion of Canada. That being the situation, where do we stand to-day? I do not know if it has appealed to hon. gentlemen as it has to me, that there was no reason that I can clearly see why the HydroElectric Commission should have come to this House. There is no sign of any kind, nor has it been contended, that the Canadian Northern railway is seeking to. gain any advantage over the Hydro-Electric Railway Commission. The Canadian

Northern railway is on this ground, it has spent nearly $2,000,000 and it has committed itself to its bond-holders. There is room for the Hydro-electric to go alongside of the Canadian Northern railway or any place else through the district, to make their own connections with any points they choose. Then why this agitation? I feel that the agitation,, is one of those unkind things that sometimes happen in public as well as in private life, they thought the Canadian Northern Railway was a good thing to hit because everybody has been hitting it, and they chase down here to attempt to stampede this Parliament on the plea that it a death blow to the Hydro. Not one of them has said so.
Sir Adam Beck said so.

The chairman of the commission endeavoured to appeal to the Railway Committee on that line. Why? Because another railway is in on the ground and is building its lines? It seems to me that the Bill is being opposed on sentiment. There is nothing in the argument against the Bill that appeals to me, or that would appeal to the reason of any *representative who gives fair, honest study to the situation and who tries to act fairly and honestly with his conscience and to the people whom he represents. It is said that the Chairman of the HydroElectric Commission is asking $100,000,000 -he puts it at $80,000,000, but other people say it will take $100,000,000-for the development of this system in welstern Ontario. A friend from eastern Ontario says that they will want another $100,000,000 in their section. There is just $200,000,000 that is being aimed at in this war time. They are very free to say that this railway is bankrupt and cannot finance new lines. But the question of financing' for the Hydro-electric is in the future, and it	does	seem to	me that in
the very near future financing may become very precarious. We do not know exactly where that $200,000,000 is going to come from; nobody tries to tell us. They tell us that the Government are going to guarantee and aid the municipalities which endorse the project. But we must not forget that this is war time. Can any man tell me how far the effect of the war will go in hindering the financing of either that or any other big scheme in this country? I look to one factor in our national life that relates to the period of reconstruction after 
the war. Can hon. gentlemen tell me how many immigrants we are going to have, having regard to the wastage in Europe of man power, having regard to the wastage in England, in Ireland and in Scotland, having regard to the upbuilding of the destroyed towns, villages, cities, countries, the very lands of Europe? It is possible that Europe will need all her mem for her own. rehabilitation. Where is our great influx of immigration to come from? Without immigration this country will be thrown upon its own resources. Our railways already constructed will be thrown upon their resources. Is it good policy to throw competition into our national railway systems, either now or just .after the war? I would say to my hon. friends opposing this Bill that they should hold themselves in patience. Our existing railways will have a hard enough row to hoe. I feel that under these circumstances we must carefully guard against inflation; we must carefully guard against undue criticism of established industries; we must carefully conserve the vested interests of this country. I am not at all afraid to use the word "interests." Some people cast it up as a slur; "Oh, he is in favour of the interests." I have met that cry on the platform and in the committee, and I have had the charge made through the press. I pay no attention to it. I stand here as a member of this House, reserving to myself my own good judgment to vote as I think right; and if my constituents feel that I have voted wrongly, it is up to them to say so, and I shall he perfectly content with their verdict. But on this question, as the father or sponsor of this Bill, I ask the Parliament of Canada here assembled to consider the principle upon which they are voting, to consider it in its broad and national scope. If that is conscientiously done, as I know it will be, I have no doubt that this House will pass this Bill as Bills of a similar nature have been passed by it from time immemorial.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is the purpose oi these charters which my hon. friend has advocated so well this afternoon, to provide for through traffic?
One of the Bills, No. 24.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They do not look so much to local traffic as to securing a channel for through traffic.
That is the main thing; feeders.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is it impossible that if the hydro-electric has a road, the same object might be gained by getting running rights over that road, and so subserve the through purposes of the Canadian Northern railway?

I should think that would be possible. Conference after conference took place. The Cfenadian Northern dropped one section of the proposed Bill. There are many things that might be done, but I am not authorized to say how far they would go towards carrying out that suggestion.

It has been rather a pleasure for me to be here this afternoon and listen to the discussion, if for nothing else than to observe the coming to life again of our old friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett). Those of us who were in this House prior to 1911 remember him very often dealing doughty blows to his opponents, but from that day until the present we have scarcely heard from him. However, I think my hon. friend sees the trend of public affairs, sees the handwriting on the wall and has come to the conclusion that he will soon be back in Opposition again, and that it is necessary for him to get into fighting trim. Therefore, he comes forward and deals some good blows to those sitting around him. We have spent a good de&l of the time of Parliament in connection with, these Bills. They were up before the Railway Committee for a number of days. My hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) says there has been more time spent on them than on any other Bill since he has been in the House. Why should all this time be spent on these Bills? There is one simple way in which the matter could be decided once and for all. What is the attitude of the Government on this question? The Government is responsible for the legislation that passes through this House and for these Bills going through or not going through. If the people of Ontario are going to be turned down by the passage of these Bills, who is it that is turning them down? The Government of Canada, representing largely as they do the province of Ontario, are the ones who have turned them down. When these Bills were before the Railway Committee there were only two things that prevented them from being defeated there. One was the rather unfortunate manner in which the case was presented by Sir Adam Beck. He had a thoroughly good case, but presented it in such a way that he spoiled it absolutely and he drove a great deal of
support away by his manner in dealing with it. The other thing that prevented the defeat of these Bills by the Railway Committee was the fact that the hon. Acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) called on the committee to vote the Bills through. He said that the Bills should pass and when the Minister of Railways goes to the Railway Committee and states that a Bill should pass, the general custom is that the Bill goes through. The Government must assume the whole responsibility whether the Hydro-Electric people get what they want or they do not get what they want. In my judgment they will not be very likely to get what they want. Did you ever know this Government, when it came to a question between the people and the big interests to stand by the people as against the big interests?
Always.

My hon. friend can
call order as much .as he likes, but that will not effect the case, because what I am stating is the absolute fact. If this proposition of the HydroElectric people of Ontario is turned down the people of Ontario will put the blame where it properly belongs and that is on the Government of Canada because they can by one word grant the wishes of the people as presented in the Railway Committee by the unanimous vote of the Legislature of Ontario. The recommendation of the Government of Ontario has the unanimous support of the Opposition.
I quite agree with my hon. friend who has just taken his seat that, because the people of one province ask for a certain thing, even unanimously, we members from different parts of the country are not absolved from exercising our opinions and carrying out our views. I think every hon. member is perfectly right in taking his own course on the matter and voting accordingly. But at the same time, when you find a province like the great province of Ontario asking this House unanimously to take a certain course, it becomes others who are not from that province to think twice before turning down huch a proposition. When the matter of free wheat was up for discussion, I thought that the representatives of those provinces more particularly interested, although I claim the whole Dominion is interested, should have had greater consideration extended to their views by this House. It is the same today. I think that the views of hon. mem-

bers representing the province of Ontario should have special consideration on a question that affects them more particularly th'an it affects the people of any other province.
These charters are fairly old; one of them is 13 years old and the other 16. In justice to Mackenzie and Mann, it must be said that they only owned one of them foi six years, and I am not sure as to how long they have owned the second one. During the first three years that they owned these charters, times were so good, money was plentiful and MacKenzie and Mann could have got all the money they wanted for any legitimate enterprise. They got a good deal of money for the development of enterprises which I would hesitate to put under that name. They could have got all the money they wanted for a proposition of this kind. They did not get it, because they did not want to go on and and my judgment is that Mackenzie and Mann do want to go on with this road to-day but want to hold up the Hydro-Electric and make them pay through the nose. Once this House passes this legislation the people of Ontario, as represented by the Hydro-Electric Commission, will pay, and pay sweetly for these charters. It becomes a question in my judgment, whether or not we should put these charters through. This is not the'first time that I have been called upon to vote against a renewal of charters, not so much against the Canadian Northern as against the Canadian Pacific. In my judgment, when any road allows a charter to hang fire and will only build a few miles just to keep somebody else from building for 13 and 16 years, it would be nothing out of our way if we said to the Canadian Northern: "The 'iLord knows you have charters enough and mileage enough to deal with, more than you have money to handle properly, and if you have any money to spend, put it in the lines that you have in other parts of the country." My hon. friend who preceded me talked about the great Canadian Northern railway from the Atlantic to the Pacific and the magnificent trains they were running. If we had happened to be on one of those through trains in the last couple of months, he would have been tied up in the snow for a month or more because in my own constituency, through which the road runs for some hundreds of miles, they were tied up at one time for 25 days.

That's an awful country.

M;r. TURRIFF: A bad country for a rusted railway to operate in, but a good country for a good railway. I admit that many parts of the Canadian Northern system are all right. They have a magnificent franchise in the Prairie Provinces, for instance, carrying a large proportion of the grain produced there; but other parts of the system, to give proper accommodation, should have had spent on them double the amount that has been expended.
There has been a great deal of discussion this afternoon of the Government's policy with regard to these radial lines. I should like to ask the Acting Minister of Railways or the Secretary of State, or whoever is leading the Government, whether it is the intention of the Government to give the radial lines a subsidy of $3,200 a mile, or any other subsidy. Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce could shed a little light on this point.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is it light that my hon. friend is after? When my hon. friend appeals for light, it is a Christian act to give him all the light we possibly can. With regard to the policy of the Government, I have heard the discussion as it has gone along, and I have not felt that it is particularly germane to that discussion what policy the Government should pursue with regard to these radial lines. I can ease my hon. friend's mind in one respect, however. I do not think any pledge has been given as to what amount shall be granted to these lines, or that it has been decided one way or the other whether aid shall be grafted.

It was well for me that it was not light I was after. If I had been asking for darkness I would have a better chance of getting it from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I had but a faint hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might, in a moment of weakness, give me a little light. However, if we can get no information from this Government on that point, Sir Adam Beck plainly stated that he had an understanding, if not a promise, that assistance would be given to these radial railways. The Hydro-Electric has cut the price of power and light in two for the people of Ontario, lust as did the city of Winnipeg whan it went into the light and power business a few years ago. Previous to that, Mackenzie and Mann charged in Winnipeg 10 cents per kilowatt hour for lighting, heating and
t

cooking. The city of Winnipeg put in theii own plant, and are now not only paying their way, but are charging only 3 cents per kilowatt hour for light, and 1 cent per kilowatt hour for heat and cooking. The Hydro-Electric in Ontario is giving cheap power to the farmers, and making conditions on the farm much better, the farmers now being able to use cheap power instead of expensive labour. And in what better way can we get cheap power to the farms than by a system of hydro-radials, the one transmission line serving both to run the radials and supply the power to the farmers? The- hydro can do this at half the price that Mackenzie and Mann would charge. The people of Ontario will get cheaper transportation on the radials than on the big railway companies. But even if the charges are as high, what profit the hydro makes will all go back into the system, with a consequent reduction in rates, and an extension of the system. Why should we hesitate to decide between the two? Did anybody ever know Mackenzie and Mann to build a line of railway anywhere in this country between the Atlantic and Pacific, without getting money from the people of Canada in subsidies and guarantees, but chiefly in gifts? They have had large guarantees from the three Prairie Provinces. The road across the prairies was very easily built, and I have no doubt it will always be able to earn interest on the money it cost, because the traffic there is considerable. But look at the position British Columbia is in to-day. Chiefly through the manipulations of the Canadian Northern, British Columbia is practically bankrupt to-day; it has guaranteed $80,000,000 of bonds, chiefly for Mackenzie and Mann, and not one mile of the roads guaranteed is able to earn operating expenses, let alone interest on the money, nor will it for many years to come. Would hon. gentlemen give to such a road as that preference over the road that the people of Ontario want? It does not seem to me a reasonable proposition. Giving the Hydro the preference would not interfere with Mackenzie and Mann to any great extent; they have a wide enough area to operate in outside of the portion of Ontario that is asking for these radials. Why not decide that the people of Ontario shall have what they want, and let Mackenzie and Mann devote their time *and attention to what they have already got. That is my view of this question, and that is how I am going to vote.

The 'Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

war continues for another year, it will be necessary for us to vote an additional $500,000,000, and even then we shall not be paying anything like our share of the war, because, when the war is over and an adjustment is made with Great Britain, we shall have to pay all the expenditure made on the other side of the water in connection with Canada's share in the war. As pre; sent conditions are different from what they were two or five or ten years ago, it is the duty of this Parliament or of this Government to put a stop once and for all to this duplication of railroads. Why allow a railroad to build if it is going to parallel another line? Why should we pick out Mackenzie and Mann and favour them to the disadvantage of the people of Ontario as represented by the Hydro-Electric Commission?
The other day the argument was advanced in the Railway Committee that in a matter of a year or two the Dominion of Canada would have to take over the Canadian Northern railway. There is absolutely no question about that. The Canadian Northern railway is to-day a bankrupt concern, and if we have to take it over in a year or two, the fewer miles of railroad we have then, the richer Canada will be, because every additional mile of railroad that we have to take over will be, not an additional asset, but an additional liability for the Government. We own 40 per cent of the common stock of the Canadian Northern railway, although I do not suppose it is worth the paper it is written on; but we own 100 per cent of the liabilities, because we have gone so far 'in bonuses and cash and land subsidies, and guarantees by the Government of Canada and guarantees by the Provincial Governments, that when that project has to be taken over under the agreement made two years ago when $45,000,000 was guaranteed to Mackenzie and Mann, we shall have to take over and shoulder all its liabilities, and every additional branch that comes in is an additional liability and not an additional asset, because Mackenzie and Mann, when they made the bargain, were too much for our astute Solicitor General, and they took care that all their properties that were good money producers were not put into the pot, but the lines of which they were not so sure were put in. The people of Ontario are ready, and willing, to take hold of those hydro-radial lines, which will give them more and better railway service, and this committee proposes to stand in the way and prevent them doing it. I want to ask the

Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who is apparently leading the House, what the policy of the Government is in connection with this road?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman had better go on with his speech. Later on, perhaps, some announcement will be made.

It is pretty hard to get any information out of the Government. My hon. friend will not say what the policy of the Government is. As my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Railways has just come in, I would ask him what the policy of the Government is in connection with this railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I will speak after a while, and I will answer that question.

We have accomplished
something at all events. If I understood the hon. gentleman aright, he is going to announce the policy of the Government. However, to announce that policy he has only to repeat here what he said in the Railway Committee, and I think he should state it here. I can remember when, a few years ago, the hon. gentleman sat on this side, and would make the rafters ring with demands for a statement of the policy of the Government on all such matters as this. And now that he is On the Government benches, I am sure that he will be as good as his word of that time, and will tell us exactly what the policy of )the Government is on this question. In the Railway Committee the other day, he said that those who proposed to build railways had to come before the Minister of Railways and Canals for approval of their plans, and that whatever he did the Government would be behind him. So that he practically assumed the full responsibility of the Government in passing or throwing out this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The hon. member was at the committee the other day. He will remember that I stated that this was a private Bill, and that it was entirely for the committee to decide what should be done. But I said also, that according to the Railway Act, before any action could be taken on any Bill passed by this Parliament, the plans had to be submitted to the Minister of Railways and Canals for his approval, and had to be submitted also to the Board of Railway Commissioners. And, of course, the Government assumes responsibility for the action of the Minister of Railways and Canals.

That is exactly what I
was saying-that the Government is absolutely responsible for the passing of this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I did not say that.

The hon. member knows as well as any member of 'this House that the Government is constitutionally responsible for all the legislation that passes in this House, and that in this respect there is no distinction between a private Bill and a Government Bill. Would the Government allow a private Bill to pass of which they did not approve? If this Bill is approve^ by this Parliament it will be through the force and command of this Government. As I have said, if the people of Ontario are turned down it will be by the Government, and the people will know who turned them down. I was glad to hear the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid,) say that the Government is responsible, because the plans must be approved by the Minister of Railways and Canals before the road can be built, and in that way the Government can stop it if they want to. But if the minister approves the plans and the road goes on it will be because it has the consent of the Government behind it. Since the House rose at six o'clock the following telegram has been received from Hon. Mr. Hearst, Premier of Ontario. It is addressed, to my hon. friend from West Peterborough:
Toronto, Ont., 3rd April, 1916.
J. H. Burnham, M.P.,
House of Commons.
Cannot understand your message.
Oh, oh.
That is extraordinary.

Do not applaud too much until you have heard the rest of it.
This Government cannot emphasize more strongly than it has done already its opposition to the extension of the Canadian Northern railway charters. Not only was our Ottawa agent authorized to oppose the Bills, but a representative was also sent from the Attorney General's Department to state the Government's opposition. And further than this, a resolution moved by the Attorney General and passed unanimously by the legislature was forwarded protesting against these renewals.
W. H. Hearst.

Should not the message of the hon. gentleman which called forth this telegram be given, that we may understand the correspondence?
155i

I simply wished that the Prime Minister of Ontario should restate definitely his position, in order to have something of the latest moment to go' upon. So I wired him, asking if the Government of Ontario opposed the extension of the Canadian Northern railway charter now before this House. His reply has been read- he cannot understand my asking, and he says, of course, that the Ontario Government oppose these Bills.

That makes it perfectly clear, if it was not perfectly clear before, that the people of Ontario are opposed to the passage of these Bills; they do not want these charters renewed. And there is no particular hardship in not renewing them. This railway company has any amount of scope for its activities in other parts of the country. At this moment, on the Goose Lake line in the West, there are hundreds of thousands of bushels of wheat lying on the open prairie, uncovered, subject to the snow and the rain, and hundreds of thousands of bushels of this grain have rotted and will become a total loss. Why? Simply because this road could not take that wheat out as soon as it was threshed last fall-could not handle it, and have not handled it. There is scope for good work for them there. Nobody else wants to put in money there. But here, where the money is ready in other hands, and the people want these roads developed, the company ask us to pass this legislation over the heads of the people of Ontario. To my mind, it is not a proper policy for this House to carry on. I do not know that I need say any more. '
Hear, hear.

There are some members of this House, so confirmed in their views, that nothing whatever can affect them, and my hon. friend who says " hear, hear," I think, is one of these; he is a fine member and has as good a right to his views as I have to mine; but my view is that this House will make a mistake if it turns down the people in favour of the corporation. But if we do so, it will be the Government that does it, and the Government must take the full responsibility for whatever action is taken by this House in connection with these Bills.

Through force of accident I have been unable to attend any of the meetings of the Railway Committee in which this Bill was discussed. As this Bill affects lines of railway proposed

to be built in the county I have the honour to represent, I feel it my duty to express my views, and, I think, the views which the people of Welland, with great unanimity, hold with regard to these Bills, and particularly with regard to Bill No. 8, which, I understand, is the Bill under discussion at the present time. I am in favour of granting these extensions and of Parliament passing this legislation. The Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Railway Company have been operating lines of electric railway in the counties of Welland and Lincoln and have been giving the greatest possible satisfaction in an excellent electric railway service. They have a line of railway extending from the town of Port Dalhousie on lake Ontario through the city of St. Catharines, the towns of Merritton, Thorold, Welland and Humber-stone to Port Colborne on lake Erie, also extending from St. Catharines through Port Weller to the town of Niagara at the mouth of the Niagara river, and from the city of St. Catharines through the town of Thorold to the city of Niagara Falis. This service meets with the entire approval of the public who are being served. They are now asking for an extension of the charter which was granted to them some years ago, and so far as I have been able to gather, the objection to this extension is that it would in some way be detrimental to the interests of the Hydro-Electric Commission or to the Government and the people of Ontario in the construction of radial lines of railway. I would not be a party to the granting of any charters which would be detrimental to the construction of radial railways by the Government of the province of Ontario or by the Hydro-Electric Commission. If I thought that the extension of this charter would be detrimental to the interests of the Hydro-Electric Commission in the construction of its lines of railway, I would take a different course, but I cannot bring, myself to believe that the construction of the lines mentioned in this Bill will have such a detrimental effect. I am inclined to think that a large part of the opposition to this Bill has arisen from the fact that hon. gentlemen are not fully acquainted with local conditions. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Turriff) said in his closing remarks that we should not grant power to the Canadian Northern against the wishes of the people who are particularly to be be served. On the other hand, if the people who live in the locality are in favour of granting the concession to the Canadian Northern, I 
assume that my hon. friend would agree that we should carry out their behest. The Municipal Councils of the city of St. Catharines, the city of Niagara Falls, the town of Thorold, and the town of Welland have, with almost complete unanimity, passed resolutions in favour of this Bill. The members of the Municipal Council of the town of Welland, where I reside, with one exception, voted in favour of the proposals embodied, in this Bill. The Municipal Council of the city of St. Catharines was unanimous in favouring these proposals, as also, I believe, was the Municipal Council of the city of Niagara Falls. All the urban municipalities, through their councils, have expressed their approval, and I believe that those councils of rural municipalities which have expressed any opinion have expressed themselves as being in favour of this Bill. What is it that is asked for? The company seeks to extend its line of railway from Port Colborne to Fort Erie, and from Fort Erie to Niagara Falls, and from Niagara Falls to the town of Niagara.
They dropped the line from Port Colborne to Fort Erie.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The Hydro-Electric Commission said that if the company would drop that part from Port Colborne to Fort Erie they would be satisfied to ajlow the Bill to pass. After that they objected.
It does not seem to be dropped in the copy of the Bill that I have, which is reprinted as amended and reported by the Railway Committee.
The company offered to drop that, but the Hydro-Electric refused. Then the company put the Bill through without making that concession, and it is in the reprint; nothing has been dropped.

I am pleased to know that it has not been dropped; I hope that it will remain in the Bill until the Bill is finally passed and receives the approval of His Royal Highness the Governor General, because that is a portion of railway which the people in that locality are anxious to have constructed and constructed speedily. The construction of the line from the town of Welland to the city of Brantford, so far as its interference with hydro-radials is concerned, might assume a different complexion, but outside of that the construction of any of the lines mentioned in this Bill would in no way interfere with the
/

construction of radial lines by the HydroElectric Commission. No general scheme for the construction of radial railways through that section of the province of Ontario has been settled on, and it will take some years to formulate and develop a scheme for the construction of such railways. The people in the locality want these lines of railway built at once, and this company pledge themselves to build them at-once. The whole coastline of the lake from Port Colborne to Fort Erie, which is a thickly settled portion of the country, is being built up with summer residences, and the people want electric railway accommodation. * The only railway accommodation which they have at the present time, or have had, is the Grahd Trunk railway, which is, of course, as good a service as a steam railway-a freight railway, practically-could give them. They give a fairly good service, but not what the people require. They want an electric service, and they want it speedily. If a hydro-electric railway is constructed through that Niagara district from Hamilton east, in the very nature of things it will necessarily come to the town of Welland, south of St. Catharines, the largest town in the district, which is getting to be a very considerable manufacturing centre. Such a line of railway would come to the town of Welland, and from there it would branch to Niagara Falls, and probably go to Fort Erie; but it would not go to the village of Port Colborne from Welland, because it wuld then be in direct competition with the line of railway of this present company. It would go to Fort Erie, passing through the centre of the district, which is a wealthy farming section, and it would accommodate the villages through that section, so there would then be no competition between the two lines. There is this further with regard to the hydro-electrics through that section or through other parts of Ontario: the Hydro-Electric Commission have now utilized all the electric current which they have a right to procure under their agreement with the Ontario Power Company. They have an agreement with the Ontario Power Company of Niagara Falls for a large amount of electric power at a fixed low price. They have utilized to the full limit all of that power, and if they had railways built at this moment they could not operate them owing to the lack of electrical current.
They have a policy for developing electric power at Chippewa.

Sir Adam Beck has suggested the development of electrical power at Chippewa. His proposition is to start at the mouth of the Welland river at the village of Chippewa, two miles above Niagara Falls, and construct a raceway thence, parallel with the Niagara river, to Queenston Heights, a distance of 10 or 12 miles. This would be virtually a canal from the mouth of the Welland river to Queenston Heights, and he proposes to there develop the electrical power. It is a gigantic scheme. Enormous electrical power could be developed by such a scheme, and possibly some time in the distant future it may be done. It could not be carried out excepting with the active co-operation of the Ontario Government. It will take years to construct. I venture . to say that no man conversant with the situation will say that that scheme can be carried out, or will be carried out, and electrical power developed under it within from 7 to 10 years. It will cost from $25,000,000 to $30,000,000, and probably more, perhaps $50,000,000. It will be an enormously expensive undertaking and will take long years in construction. To hold up the construction of electric railways through that district, depending on the possible chance of the Ontario Government ever constructing this hydro-electric development, would be an outrage on the people of that locality. No hydro-electrics can be operated or will be operated in that Niagara district by the Hydro-Electric .Commission until they have formulated and carried out a scheme of electrical power development, either on the lines already suggested by Sir Adam Beck or on some other lines, that will give them sufficient power to operate those railways. The people of that locality are anxious that these lines shall be built and built at once. The project has met with the approval of the people there. I have yet to learn that any municipal council of that district ha? disapproved of the passing of this Bill. Resolutions have been passed stating that the Bill should not d>e passed if its passing would interfere with the construction of the hydro-radial lines; but I contend, and I think that every hon. gentleman must see, that the construction of these lines cannot possibly interfere in any way with the construction of hydro(-eledtric radial lines. This ie the wealthiest section of the province of Ontario. It has become an enormous manufacturing centre, and its

manufacturing importance will increase as years go toy. Is the Hydro-Electric Commission to have an absolute monopoly of the whole district? Is it to build lines over that whole district to the absolute exclusion of their construction by companies which are already operating there? If this was an absolutely new company, with no financial interests there, there might be some argument against the granting of the charter. But here is a company which has been operating electric lines there for many years, which has given and is giving entire satisfaction to the people. Then I say they should be allowed to construct these lines, in view of the probability that if they are not allowed to construct them there can be no construction for six or seven or ten years, by reason of the fact that even if they are constructed the Hydro-Electric Commission will have no current to operate them. For these reasons I trust that this committee will report this Bill, and that it will receive the approval of Parliament.

Mr. Chairman, it is with a great
"deal of diffidence that I rise to offer a few observations on this much-discussed subject; but as the matter is one of principle, I feel constrained to trespass on the patience of the House in reference to it. There is no doubt that the people of Canada are enor-* mously interested in the success of the Canadian Northern railway. There is no doubt that the' people of Canada, and particularly of Ontario, are vitally interested in this question of electrical development and of the extension of hydro-electric railways. The province of Ontario, through its legislature, has asked this House not to pass this legislation, and has also sent a representative to the Railway Committee to oppose it. So it seems reasonable for a moment to consider on what ground the province takes this position of hostility. The ownership of the stock of the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Railway Company is quite immaterial in the discussion of this Bill, because the stock might as well be owned by John Smith or William Jones or any one else. The ownership has nothing to do with it. We have before us a Bill of the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Railway Company. What does it ask? It asks authority to build a line from Port Colborne to Fort Erie, and Fort Erie to the city of Niagara Falls; from the city of Niagara Falls to the town of Niagara; from the town of Welland to the city of Brantford; an extension of the

line of the St. Catharines and Niagara Central Railway Company to a point on the Niagara river at Fort Erie.
All of this is of a distinctly local nature. The question naturally arises: what on earth is a railway of a purely local character doing here with the Dominion Parliament, and why is it that we are here legislating in reference to a matter of that kind? It certainly was never intended by the British North America Act, as far as I can understand it, that the legislature of the Dominion should be bothered with these local matters. It was always intended that street railways should be dealt with by cities; that municipalities should deal with their local matters, counties with theirs, and provinces with theirs. Perhaps for a moment it would do no harm to go back to first principles, and call the attention of the committee to section 92 of the British North America Act, which gives exclusive powers to Provincial Legislatures on certain subjects. The exclusive powers of the Provincial Legislatures in relation to railways come under subsection 10:
Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province.
Where they are within the province they are local works and undertakings, and the province has exclusive jurisdiction over them unless the Dominion under subsection (b) declares the particular local works to be for the general advantage of Canada. When this charter was passed there was strenuous opposition to it on the ground of provincial rights. Those of us who opposed it at that time, believed in provincial rights, and said that the Legislature of Ontario should have had the right to incorporate and deal with this railway. Those of us who opposed it at that time believing in provincial rights and believing that the Legislature of Ontario should have the right to incorporate this company and deal with this railway, resisted this legislation. But the Parliament of Canada, for reasons which I have never been able to understand, except that there was a wonderful lobby put up, declared it to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. It was not a transcontinental railway in any sense nor did it connect with any transcontinental railway. There was absolutely no more reason for it than that the promoters of the Bill did not want to go to the Ontario Legislature, believing as they did that in face of its elec-

trical railway legislation they could do better in Ottawa where they could get members from other parts of Canada to vote for it much, more easily than they could get it through the Ontario Legislature. It was under such circumstances that this charter came into existence. The position of the matter to-day is that unless the Dominion Parliament reaffirm that this is a work for the general advantage of Canada and gives new life to this particular charter, it is dead and gone.
The suggestion has been made that there are vested rights to be considered. When a railway is given a license to build within a definite time and does not exercise that license there is no such thing as a vested right. There is an absolute license to build, but if the license is not exercised it does not become a vested right. If it is exercised, of course, there is a vested right. Our statutes are carefully drawn The statute says that in so far as this railway is constructed within the powers granted by the charter it shall be valid, and that as regards any portion not constructed that shall be null and void and there shall be no further power. We are told that there are innocent bondholders. Those who try to raise money for the construction of railways will have to go a long way to find an innocent bondholder who does not look over the Act and have it examined by his counsel, and who does not know that if the company do not have enough money to build the whole line he will have very poor security for his money, and that if he loans money under such circumstances he takes a risk. That being so, there is no vested right, there is no innocent bondholder who is affected, and the question comes down to what should be done in the public interest. Since the inception of this railway, and since this charter has practically lapsed, there has arisen in Ontario a desire on the part of the people of that province to have railways owned and operated by the province or by the Hydro-Electric Commission. We all have to bow to these changes in public sentiment and if this charter had been before the Legislature where it belongs, that Legislature would not have come down here with telegrams and deputations asking us to hold our hands, but would be attending to its own business in dealing with this legislation. This legislation may be here by an accident of fortune but surely as members of this House there is an obligation resting upon us to treat the province of Ontario, or anv other province, with the
consideration it deserves. If we are satisfied that this charter has to do with a local work, a local undertaking within the province of Ontario, if we find that it is something that should not be dealt with by this Parliament, 'the obligation rests upon us, Hot to renew this charter but to leave this railway where it belongs.
I have nothing to say against the Canadian Northern railway. We are vitally interested in that railway. We must be fair to every railway and to every vested interest. But, this is a purely local matter, and we have the province of Ontario, by a unanimous vote, requesting us to leave it in the position in which it is to-day. Apart from what the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) has said, no one has suggested that any municipality outside of St. Catharines has been asking for this legislation. I do not know whether this information is correct or not but assuming that it is, has 'any one else to-day suggested that any other municipality has been asking for this legislation?
The council of Welland has asked for it with absolute unanimity, with only one exception.
I am speaking so far as my information goes.
Three municipalities sent word to the Chairman of the Committee by telegram.

That may be so, but I have noticed in Hansard an enormous list of municipalities which are objecting to this legislation apart from the provincial authorities, and apart from the HydroElectric Commission. When we are getting objections of that character, I say that the obligation rests upon us to consider fairly and squarely the merits of the situation and to vote, each one of us, in accordance with what we believe to be in the public interest. For myself, I can only say that I have not yet heard anything that makes me believe that a renewal of this charter is essential to the Canadian Northern as [DOT]a transcontinental railway. It appears to me to be a purely local line, and I believe that the Hydro-Electric Commission, if they are going to operate in this district, should have a monopoly and should not have competition. I cannot see for one moment why, if the people have the right to charter railways they should not have a monopoly if they want one, because the granting of these charters is an act of public

grace. It is the public which give these charters, and the public takes them away if they determine they must have a monopoly for 'the carrying on of their affairs. I think that before we consider the renewal of this charter, or before we do anything more in this regard, we should do a little stocktaking in connection with railway construction in this country. We have great national obligations at the present time. I would not propose to refuse absolutely the granting of all extensions, but I do say that before an extension is granted to any line we should have a report from the Railway Commission, or from some competent body, as to what the rights of the parties in respect to the constructions of these particular utilities are, and how the country or the province is affected by a further expenditure in connection with that construction. I say that we should take stock of the situation and see how the country is going to come out in connection with the matter.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to prolong the discussion, but I want to answer a few questions that have been asked during the afternoon and to call attention to an amendment that I have, to offer. I hope the House will accept the amendment, so that it may come up for discussion to-morrow night. An hon. gentleman who spoke this afternoon called attention to the fact that having voted $45,000,000 by way of assistance to1 the Canadian Northern railway we were interfering with the protection of our rights if we refused the extension of this charter. All I can say is that I was one of those who took part in ihat proceeding, and I have nothing to apologize for. I am satisfied that it was the proper thing for us to do under the circumstances, but I believe that the time has come when we should call a halt to the granting of concessions in the -way of guarantees of 'bonds. I merely wish to call attention to the financial position in which the Canadian Northern railway is placed. I feel that I should do this owing to the fact that the statements have been made this afternoon in regard! to Canadian Northern finances. We have been told that they are perfectly able to carry on this undertaking which is going to cost some $13,000,000. I believe that this statement which I shall read should be placed on Hansard	so that	members on

both sides of the House may be made aware of the Condition of the finances of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I may say that the statement has been compiled at my request by the (Statistical Branch of the Department of Railways and Canals within the last week or ten days, and I can vouch for'its accuracy. It covers the fourteen different companies under the management of the< Canadian (Northern railway, and it says:
The situation for the year ended 30th June, 1914, according to sworn returns to the Department of Railways and Canals, was as follows :
Bonds of the various steapi railways owned and operated by Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann were outstanding to the amount of $255,664,197.
There were, in addition to the foregoing, bonds outstanding on lines under construction to the amount of $40,209,330.
At 4 per cent, which is a normal rate, the interest charges on the operating lines would amount to $10,226,568. The actual payment of taxes wras $371,429. There were other charges, such as rents for leased lines, which amounted to $693,167. These items combined make a total of $11,291,164.
As the net operating revenue was only $7,635,693, it will he seen that there was a deficit for the year of $3,655,471, which had to be met out of borrowings.
The real deficit was undoubtedly larger. Every soundly conducted railway must make large deductions from revenue for additions and betterments. None were made in the foregoing statement.
The Canadian Northern proper had a met credit balance for the year of $184,509. The deficit was created by the subsidiary roads, although the $184,509 to the credit of the Canadian Northern make no allowance for betterments out of revenue. If a proper allowance for that purpose had been made, there would have been a considerable deficit too.
In 1915 the situation, from the standpoint of accounting, was materially changed. Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann were permitted by legislation to make a consolidated report for their various railway interests. This report included all their steam lines, the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Electric line, their express and telegraph interests, their hotels, steamers, and so on. Some of these outside operations, particularly the express business, had always shown considerable profits. All the accounts, good and bad, were brought together under the head of the Canadian Northern railway system.
For this Canadian Northern railway system, the bond liability was placed at $315,921,374! At 4 per cent the interest charges would he $12,636,855, to which should he added taxes $454,227, rents for leased lines $351,460 and other interests $70,604

making a total of $13,513,146 for fixed charges. As the corporate income of the system, or the difference between gross earnings and operating expenses, was but $7,222,692, it will be seen that there was an immediate deficit of $6,290,454 for the year. This shortage, of course, had to be met out of borrowings.
The Canadian Northern railway system is very poorly equipped. For example, it had

last year an average of 346'5 freight cars per 100 miles of line, as against 1,144"0 by the Canadian Pacific. It would require a very large capital expenditure, certainly far in excess of $100,000,000, to bring the physical standard of the Canadian Northern up to the standard of a first-class railway.
The Canadian Northern, then, have less than one-third the number of freight cars the Canadian Pacific railway have, per 100 miles. I am placing these figures on record so that the House may see how important it is to give these Bills our most careful consideration 'before granting an extension of the charters.
It was my privilege to he one of the joint chairmen of the committee that considered the consolidation of the Railway Act two years ago. That committee's work included a careful investigation of the clauses which deal with the lines that are about to be built, and the amendment I propose is a copy, to a very large extent, of the clauses in the Railway Act which have reference to the commencement of work, and the location of the line. I believe that I am voicing the opinion of Sir Adam Beck, and of the Government of Ontario, when I ask the House to accept the following amendment:
That the following clause be added to Bill 8, An Act respecting the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Railway Company:
The company shall not commence the construction of any of the railways herein mentioned, or any section or portion of any such railway, until the general location of such railway has been approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners as hereinafter provided, nor until the plans, profiles and books of reference of such railway have been sanctioned by and deposited with the board and duly certified copies thereof deposited with the registrars of deeds, in accordance with the provisions of the Railway Act.
The company shall prepare and submit to the board, in duplicate, a map showing the general location of each proposed line of railway, the terminal and the' principal towns and places through which the railway is to pass, giving the names thereof, the railways, navigable streams and tide-waters, if any, to be crossed by the railway, and such as may be within a radius of thirty miles of the proposed railway, and, generally, the physical features of the country through which the railway is to be constructed, and shall give such further or other information as the board may require.
Such map shall be prepared upon a scale not smaller than six miles to the inch, or upon such other appropriate scale as the board may determine, and shall be accompanied by an application in duplicate requesting the board's approval of the general location as shown on the said map.
The board may approve such map and location, or any portion thereof, or may make or require such changes and alterations therein as it deems expedient; but if the board deems that
the construction of such railway upon the proposed location or upon any portion thereof is not in the public interest it shall refuse approval of the whole or of such portion, and in any case where the board deems it in the public interest it may, as to any portion of the proposed railway, make and order, or require the taking of any proceedings, provided for by section 176 of the Railway Act.
Where the board approves the whole or any portion of such map and location such approval shall be signified upon the map and the duplicate thereof accordingly.
The map when so approved and the application shall be filed in the Department of Railways and- Canals and the duplicate thereof with the board.
You will notice that the Board of Railway Commissioners will have absolute control of the whole matter. I am satisfied that similar clauses should be included in every charter that is granted by this Parliament from this time forth, and I am sure that the Board of Railway Commissioners, which is an independent body, will be able to decide definitely what is in the best interest of the country and will investigate matters thoroughly as it will have the power to investigate under these clauses. Therefore, I move:
That the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Mr. GREEN moved concurrence in an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 11, respecting the British America Nickel Corporation, Limited.
In what does the Bill as amended differ from the Bill as passed by the House of Commons?

I think I can explain, because my attention was called to the matter when it came from the Senate. The Bill, as passed, provided that the shareholders might elect certain members of the board of directors to be an executive committee. For some reason the Senate struck out that clause. It seemed to me merely to affect the inner government of the company, but you, Mr. Speaker, thought it should be referred to the committee, and this was done with the general concurrence of the House.

I would call attention to the fact that while the Bill provides that a majority of the company's directors shall be British subjects, as is customary, it goes on to state, in section 3:
The shareholders of the company may by a resolution passed by a vote of those present, or represented by proxy and holding not less than two-thirds of the issued capital stock represented, at a general meeting called for that purpose, authorize the directors to delegate any

of their powers to an executive committee consisting of not less than three to be elected by the directors from among their number.
So that while this American company conforms to a rule that the majority of the directors must be British subjects, they provide that these directors may appoint an executive committee and delegate to them any or all of the powers of the directors.

Will the minister be
kind enough to explain why he does not make the sale of the liquor an offence by the party in the province from which it is shipped? The language of this Bill does not get after the merchant or dealer who sells liquor. I would suggest that the merchant who exports liquor into a province where there is a prohibitory law should be liable provided he sells it. The sale itself ought to be an offence as well the the sending it. The word "send" is a peculiar word to use in that sense and I think the act of selling liquor by a wholesale merchant, for example, in the city of Monte real, where it is legal to sell it in that province, to a merchant in Nova Scotia where there is a prohibitory law should be made an offence under the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL. LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
In the ordinary course the person who sells, exports the liquor, sends it, or ships it, or in some' manner provides to have it reach his customer in the prohibitory province. Where he does that he will come under the provisions of this Bill. I am not prepared to say offhand that it might not be desirable to modify it in the line suggested by the hon. gentleman. But what strikes one at first glance is that the only person who is not affected by this Bill now will be that man who confines himself to making a pure and simple sale in a non-prohibitory province. He will not be able to sell his goods, he will not be able to convey his goods, or get them into a prohibitory province without violating this law. I do not see the necessity of what is suggested although there might be a combination of circumstances where such a provision might be made to meet a case that the words here do not meet. But at first glance I think we have covered every co-operation for the violation of the law in the province into which liquor is sent by the wording which
we have provided. This is a wording similar to the wording of a provision of the Canada Temperance Act in regard to the sending, shipping, or carrying of liquor into a district which has been brought under the operation of that Act. .
