I have no doubt it will do that to some extent, and in so far as it does, it meets with my entire approval. For my part, however, I would much prefer to see the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver placed upon the statute-book, as I believe it would have given effect to the wishes of the majority of the people in this country, and had I been here I should have certainly voted for the resolution of my hon. friend. I can support this Bill only because it is a step in the right direction. I would much rather it had been broader and that prohibition had been made Dominion-wide.

In view of the many extraordinary statements that have appeared in the newspapers, perhaps the minister would give us the assurance that if the provinces should enact what they appear to want to enact, namely a full measure of prohibition, this Bill gives them eveTy opportunity of so doing. It is a strange thing that many even of the temperance papers, such as the Pioneer o: Toronto, should persistently, and almost wilfully, I think, misrepresent the views of the House in -this matter by asserting that this House, having defeated the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver, has refused to endorse the principle of prohibition; and that as a consequence the provinces cannot enact prohibition, and that if they do, it will simply be landing a number of people high and dry, and the measure turn out to be no prohibition after all.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The motive that prompted the introduction of this Bill was the belief that by this method we were going to secure to each province in this Dominion of Canada, and, if all the provinces wanted it, to secure to them all, a prohibition law going in each province just as far as the people of that province want to go, and a law which, going that far, we felt convinced would be more susceptible of effective enforcement than any law enacted 'by this Parliament imposing the will

of this Parliament upon each one of the provinces. Any province-and I have no hesitation in giving this as my opinion after the most careful examination I have been able to give to the subject-that want a really effective prohibition within its own limits and that will exercise the power which it enjoys for that purpose, will, under the operation of this measure, find iv self perfectly protected from interference with the operation of that law coming from people in any other province. What we feel is that the basis of the argument advanced in support of the proposal for a general prohibitive law was that the people of' the different provinces had given conclusive evidence that they wanted an effective prohibitory law, and evidence was adduced, in support of that proposition which certainly demonstrated a widespread desire" in all of the provinces, some going a little further than others, for effective prohibitory measures. That demonstration justifies us in assuming that the people in those provinces will see to it that their legislatures give to them just that measure of prohibition which they are prepared for and are ready to have carried out, and to see that it is carried out. If those provinces do that, by this Bill we are furnishing the protection against the bringing about of the violation of the law within the province by people who, being outside of the province that enacts the law, are not amenable to its legislative enactments.

The weak spot in the position which the Minister of Justice assumes in connection with this measure, when he states that it is the desire of the Government to go just as far as the people of the provinces desire, is that he has omitted from his Bill any prohibition of the manufacture of intoxicating liquors within the provinces in which prohibitory legislation has been or is about to be passed, the provinces themselves have no power to prohibit the manufacture of intoxicating liquors.
Yes they have, for use within the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They have very large powers.

For use within the province, but they have no power to prohibit the manufacture of intoxicating liquors within the province for export from the province, and it is the opinion of those who -are earnestly supporting prohibitory
laws that, so long as the manufacture is permitted within the provinces a prohibitory liquor law will be more or less of a dead letter. It is within the jurisdiction of this Government to prohibit the manufacture within the provinces, and if the Government desires to go upon this question as far as all the provinces desire, I am satisfied that a large majority of the people of the province of Ontario from which 1 come desire that the manufacture as well as the sale of intoxicating liquor be at the present time prohibited. There is nothing in this Bill which seeks to interfere in the least with the manufacture of intoxicating liquor within the provinces.
Would you stop its manufacture for export out of the province?

Had I been in the House I would have supported the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) which provided for the prohibition of the manufacture, sale, and importation of intoxicating liquor, and in order to make this Bill satisfactory to the provinces, my hon. friend the minister should make it go as far as I have indicated. From the way the people have voted in some provinces and petitioned in others, there is no doubt as to what the provinces desire.
Mr. R. B. BEiNNETT:	No province has
voted -against the manufacture.

Because no province has the power to prohibit manufacture for export. If the Government desires to go as far as the provinces wish it to go, then it should go further than it has gone in this Bill and include a section to prohibit altogether the manufacture of intoxicating liquors in provinces which have passed prohibitory liquor laws ot in provinces which adopt the law which this House sees fit to pass in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman lays down too wide a proposition altogether when he says that the provinces have no power to prohibit the manufacture.
For export.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When the question as
to whether the provinces had that power was put to their Lordships of the Privy Council, they answered it in the affirmative, putting this restriction; that it must depend upon the conditions and the circumstances xmder which the manufacture was carried on, so that, if the manufacture within the province would it effect constiaaVISED EDITION

tute a local evil or an impediment in the way of the province's exercising the power which the Privy Council fully recognized to the provinces, of legislating upon the question of the suppression of the use of intoxicating liquor regarded as a local evil, then the legislation would be effective. Is there any province that has prohibited the manufacture to the extent to which the Privy Council points out they are free to do it?

Not that I am aware of, because, as I say, the impression in the provinces is that they have no power to prohibit the manufacture, but there is no doubt that in this Parliment we have that power. This Government has the power and the question is: Will this Government exercise that power?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The question is this:
we are dealing with liquor as an evil within this country. An appeal has been made to us to protect the people of this country from the evils of liquor, and_we are told that the provinces want, although they have never legislated as far as lies within their power, the kind of law that will prevent the manufacture going on within a building standing in the province. That is the .one evil that the province cannot themselves correct. So far as the manufacturing may lead to one man in the province getting a drink, the province can protect itself against that. Now, all that is asked, even on the contention of the hon. gentleman as I understand it, the thing that there would be need for us to step in to do, would be to see to it that there should not exist an establishment in which liquor was manufactured, even though every drop of that liquor went out of this country.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well,_ what is the evil to be abated within this country, if the liquor (manufactured all goes out of the country? Are we so much interested in preventing the people in countries where the consumption of liquor is not looked upon as it may be looked upon amongst us, from procuring a supply from people in Canada? What injury to the temperance of the people of Canada is going to result from that fact? It does seem to me that it will be time enough for us to undertake to protect the people of other countries when the provinces have done what lies within their power to protect the people within their own limits. I can see no reason why the province is not entitled to protect its own people

from the consequences, if they be evil, inuring to the people of the province from the fact that the manufacture of liquor goes on therein. I fail to see that they have not got the power to protect their own people.
Will the hon. gentleman give the province power to prohibit the manufacture?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
proceeds upon the assumption that this Government can give power to the provinces.
By amending the British North America Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But this Parliament
cannot amend the British North America Act. We could ask the Imperial authorities to do so. But does it not occur to the hon. gentleman that if the provinces need more power perhaps they (might ask for an amendment extending tlheir power? Why should we ask an extension of power to provinces that they have not chosen to exert to the full extent-to provinces that have never expressed a desire for any extension of their power? Surely, it is a peculiar thing that we should be asked to go to the British Parliament to ask them to give the provinces greater powers than they have.

I do not see the meaning of this argument. It strikes me that it would be quite within our power to pass legislation enabling the province to prohibit the manufacture of intoxicating liquors if they chose to do so. What we should have to do would be to pass legislation saying that when a province prohibits the manufacture of intoxicating liquors that Act shall be valid. We are taking the first step now, we are prohibiting the sending of liquor into the province in which the import is forbidden. I submit that we can do the same thing so far as the manufacturer is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Wre are not now creating an offence in one province which will not be an offence in another province. The offence we are creating is one that will be an offence throughout the Dominion.
I beg pardon-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman thinks otherwise, he entirely misapprehends the Bill. Anywhere in Canada, it will be an offence for a man to send liquor

into a province where there is a law against it.
But not in any province where there is no prohibitory law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a condition of the offence, but it is a Dominion-wide law.
It does not apply to British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It applies absolutely
to the province of British Columbia. It will be the same offence for a man in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario or Nova Scotia, to send liquor into a prohibitory province to be used in violation of these laws. Let us not be misunderstood; we are making no law that will be effective in the province as a provincial law, and we give absolutely no powers to any provinces. We lay down what looks to me like the very justifiable proposition, that hereafter it shall be an offence for a man to conspire-if I may use the word-to contribute to the bringing about of the violation of the provincial law, even though he does that conspiracy, or contributing, or initiation of the offence, somewhere outside of the province whose law is violated. We .are constituting an absolutely new offence. The offence does not consist in the violation by anybody of any provincial law-because the man we are hitting is the man who is not bound by the provincial law,-but in a violation of our law. We say that it is an immoral thing, and ought to be prohibited, for a man anywhere within this Dominion deliberately to become a party to a violation, which is to take place within a province, of a law that that province has lawfully made. We give no power to the province, and we are not legislating for a particular province. The bon. gentleman suggests that we should legislate in ratification of the laws of the provinces. But if the view is right that the province cannot prohibit the manufacture, our ratification will not make valid the law that they could not make. Our power comes from the British North America Act, and we have no power of delegation-absolutely none. We can no ' more delegate to the province than the province can delegate to us. If a province should consent that we should legislate about property and civil rights in that province, we should have no more power to pass that legislation than we have now. Hon. gentlemen must understand that it
156J
has been authoritatively-"and I think once [DOT]for all-settled, that neither this Parliament nor any of the legislatures, in the exercise of its legislative functions, is exercising delegated powers. As the Privy Council has said: Provided the subject matter of the legislation comes within the subjects laid down as a proper matter for provincial legislation, the provincial legislature has the plenitude of power of the British Parliament as fully' as the British Parliament could exercise it or could confer it upon anybody else. It is an entire mistake to suppose that this Parliament stands in a position of .superiority to the provincial legislatures and hands out powers to them.
We do not contend that on this side.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
opened by saying that we ought to confer powers upon the legislatures to do these things. The second thing that I do not think it is in our power to do is to submit our legislation upon a subject matter which belongs to us-if it does not belong to us there is no occasion for our dealing with it. Assuming that we alone have the right to prohibit the manufacture, then we must prohibit that manufacture looking at the thing from a Dominion point of view. When we say: we will abdicate our function and say that whenever a legislature prohibits manufacture in a particular province, then it shall be unlawful to manufacture within that province-that is not Dominion legislation. We are no longer legislating for the peace, order and good government of Canada; and we are endeavouring to give some sort of sanction to unconstitutional legislation. We must assume it to be such: it is on the assumption that it is such that it is suggested that we ought to do the legislating. That is not exercising our functions; that is subjecting the exercise of our powers to the will of particular provinces and proceeding to make different laws for different provinces according as the legislatures of those provinces decide, and accepting the decision of the legislatures of these respective provinces upon a matter with which they have no competency to deal.

Do I understand the
minister to mean that a provincial legislature could prohibit the manufacture of liquor for use within the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that certainly
they could.

Assuming that the province of Ontario believes in prohibition, under the law which the minister proposes it would be illegal to import even a gallon of cider into the province of Ontario. If the legislature prohibit manufacture for sale within the province, would it not be right for this Parliament in that event to go further and prohibit its manufacture entirely within the province? You see how inconsistent it is to prohibit the importation of a gallon of cider and to allow millions of dollars' worth of whisky to be manufactured right in the prohibition province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When the province
will have legislated that whisky is not to be consumed in the province, then our law will prevent whisky being sent in.
It will not prevent its being manufactured, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think there is a most extraordinary misapprehension about this power to prohibit the manufacture. Their Lordships of the Privy Council, when the question was put to them, premised that they did not mean to be bound by their answers, because the question was put to them in purely academic form. This is just how they dealt with these two questions of manufacture and importation:
Their lordships must further observe that these questions being in their nature academic rather than judicial are better fitted for the consideration of the officers of the Crown than of a court of law. The replies to be given to them will necessarily depend upon the circumstances in which they may arise for decision ; and these circumstances are in this case left to speculation. It must therefore be understood that the answers which follow are not meant to have and cannot have the weight of a judicial determination, except in so far as their lordships may have occasion to refer to the opinions which they have already expressed in discussing the seventh question.
The seventh question was the question as to the validity of section 18 of the Ontario Act, prohibiting sales by retail and restricting sales by wholesale. Here is the answer to question 3:
In the absence of conflicting legislation by the Parliament of Canada their lordships are of opinion that the provincial legislation would have jurisdiction to that effect if it were shown that the manufacture was carried on under such circumstances and conditions as to make its prohibition a merely local matter in the province.
Their lordships dealt with prohibition as being merely a local matter in the province. This principle they recognized both in the provincial prohibition case and in the case

submitted with regard to the law of Manitoba. I am not suggesting that this Parlia-ment_ has not power; if it be considered that the question should be dealt with as a national evil and in the same way in all the provinces, I do not dispute the power of this Parliament to do it. But what their Lordships clearly held was, that while it might be dealt with as a national evil by the Parliament of Canada, looking at it from a Dominion standpoint, and that wherever the Parliament of Canada did deal with the question, they necessarily ousted any legislative competency of the province; in the absence of such legislation by Parliament, the provinces, looking at the suppression of the abuse or use of liquor as the abatement of a local evil, had full power to' legislate for the abatement of that local evil. If the manufacture should be carried on under such conditions as to make its suppression necessary to the abatement of a local evil, which in express terms the legislatures are held to have power to abate, I would have no doubt, so far as one can venture to say that he has no doubt with regard to any question of law, that the manufacture might be prohibited by the province itself. However, it is not, perhaps, necessary for us to go that far at the moment. What we are concerned with is bringing about the protection of Canada from the evils that result from the abuse of intoxicating beverages. Many people think that the use and the abuse are inseparable, and that therefore the only way to protect against the abuse is to do away with the use. But it is to be pointed out that none of our provinces have ever undertaken to legislate against the use of intoxicating liquor. A great many of the difficulties that seemed to exist when these questions were new questions came from the fact that the object struck at in so-called prohibitory legislation was-and has always been-the traffic in liquor. No legislative body has taken upon itself to legislate against the use of liquor.
If you stop the manufacture and sale you stop the use of liquor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Some people believe that the supply creates the demand, and some, perhaps the majority, believe that the demand creates the supply. What I should suggest is that if you want to suppress the use perhaps you would get at it more effectively if you not only suppressed the supply but went on and suppressed the very thing you want to suppress. Why has it not been dime directly? I am not sug-

gesting that you should not, if you want to get effective prohibition, prohibit the traffic, but why have the provinces stopped there?
Does the minister suggest that the provinces should enact legislation making it a crime for a man to drink intoxicating liquor?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They cannot make it a crime because they cannot make criminal law; but if, in their judgment, the use of liquor is locally, within their limits, an evil calling for abatement, I have no doubt they can legislate against the use of liquor, and when they do so our law will protect their legislation against the use of liquor. What I wanted to point out is that it is because this legislation in the past has been directed against the liquor traffic that there has been the great confusion as to the relative powers of Parliament and the provinces. When the question was originally put forward, the attack upon provincial legislation was based upon the suggestion that it was an interference with the Dominion's power with regard to the regulation of trade and commerce, and the Privy Council said that it was not a question of regulating trade and commerce but a question of abating an evil, and if one province looks upon the use of liquor as an evil, producing injurious consequences to its population, giving rise to disorder and tumult and making more difficult the enforcement of police regulations and the maintenance of order and peace within the province, that province, without getting into' the field of criminal legislation has power-and the Privy Council has so decided-to legislate to abate the evil. If the legislation had gone direct to the use of liquor you would have wiped out at one stroke all the questions that arose as to whether or not this was regulating trade and commerce. Those questions have disappeared now. I think it is safe for us to say that the decisions of the Privy Council make it clear that prohibitory law is not a matter of regulation of trade and commerce. The power of this Dominion to pass such a law rests, I think, in the last analysis, upon our power to enact criminal law.

I am in favour of a measure like this. That is to say, the Dominion Parliament should aid the provinces in enforcing prohibition. The difficulty is that it is most discouraging to the temperance people of all the provinces, while they have
prohibition against the import, to have manufacturing carried on on a large scale. Would the minister be willing to embody m this Bill a provision that it shall be unlawful to carry on the manufacture of intoxb eating liquor in any provinces where the use of it is prohibited by the local legislature?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not prepared to say yes to that right off, because if the use of it be prohibited in a province, can it be said to be legislation ancillary to that if we should prohibit the manufacture for use outside of the province?

The minister admits that it is ancillary to a prohibition of the use of it, or even prohibition of the sale of it, to prevent the import into the province in the smallest quantity. Therefore would it not be equally ancillary to a prohibition of the use of it to prevent its manufacture in that province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it be shown that the manufacture in the province leads to use in the province.
You know it will, always.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But if that be shown, then the province can attend to it itseii.
Then you would not assist the province by any legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because it would not need my assistance.
But suppose there ie some doubt; what would be the harm in putting it beyond the shadow of a doubt?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What is the usefulness?

There could be no doubt in my mind, because a manufacturer would always say that he wae manufacturing for use outside the province and then the manufacture would be legal; he could then dispose of as much as he liked in the province.

The Minister of Justice knows that the great trouble in enforcing prohibition in a province ie that liquor will be imported for illegal purposes and, in the same way, if in a prohibition province you have the manufacture carried on on a large scale, there will be the illegal use and the illegal sale of it through connivance between persons who will not hesitate to violate the law, and the manufacturers.
Just as in local option districts.
If this first section passes I propose to submit two additional clauses to the Bill. While these amendments will not go as far as the hon. gentleman suggests, yet they deal with the same point.
How far will you go?

My first amendment
reads:
In addition to any other penalties prescribed for a violation of section one of this Act, any person holding: a license to carry on the business or trade of a distiller or brewer issued under the provisions of the Inland Revenue Act who violates the provisions of section one of this Act, or who sells or delivers intoxicating liquor in violation of the law in force in any province, shall also be liable, in any prosecution under this Act, on conviction for a first offence, to the suspension of such license for any period not exceeding three months, and, on conviction for a second offence, to the suspension of his license for any period not exceeding six months, and, on conviction for a third offense, shall forfeit his license and shall thereafter be unable to hold such a license.
That does not seem to bring it within the section of the law.

It does not go as far as my hon. friend suggests, but it does this: Assuming a province passes a prohibitory law and there is a tendency on the part of a manufacturer to sell in that province contrary to the law, then this clause will provide for the cancellation o'f that manufacturer's license absolutely.
No, pardon me, the whole section is directed against the illegal sending of liquor into another province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, the hon. member's amendment, if adopted, while perhaps it would not go as far as the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John, would bring about this result: that the manufacturer holding a license from the Inland Revenue Department of this Government, who sold within the province in violation of the provincial law would suffer forfeiture of his inland revenue license, and so would be unable to carry on the manufacture.

Perhaps I may as well read the other amendment and then it will all be before the committee for discussion. The next clause as proposed will be clause . 3 of the Bill as amended if these are adopted:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence-

I understand that " indictable " will have to be deleted. I will leave that for the Minister of Justice to consider:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable on summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars, or to imprisonment for six months, or to both fine and imprisonment, who:-
(a)	sends or ships by any public conveyance to any place in which the sale of intoxicating liquor is prohibited any package containing intoxicating liquor not plainly labelled so as to show the actual contents of such package; or
(b)	sends or ships by any public conveyance any package containing intoxicating liquor-addressed to a fictitious person or addressed otherwise than to the actual consignee of such package; or
(c)	being a common carrier or the servant or agent of a common carrier, knowingly receives for conveyance, carries or makes delivery of any such package; or
(d)	knowingly takes delivery from any common carrier of any such package.
I beg to give notices of these clauses.
Mir. (Pugsley: The minister will agree with me that the amendments suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) are of very great importance and worthy of careful consideration. It is now eleven o'clock and my hon. friend the member for Bona-venture (Mr. Marcil) would like to speak on this subject. I am sure that my hon. friend will agree that copies of these proposed amendments should be struck off so that they will be distributed to members. It will be interesting to have them and, as the hon. gentleman has read them, they will be printed in Hansard.
Why could we not pass clause 1?

I was going to suggest
this to the minister. I have every desire to lend my assistance to making the Bill better if it is possible to improve it. I am a very great believer in having prohibitory legislation passed by the provinces and then have this Parliament render to the provinces by legislation whatever assistance can be rendered in the way of enabling them to better enforce the prohibitory law. If I were to express my opinion on the question at present before the House, it would be that I am wedded to local option, to having the smaller communities in the Dominion decide for themselves whether they will have a prohibitory law or not. I quite agree with what the minister stated that it is desirable 'to have public sentiment behind a prohibitory law. Until you have that to support you it will be impossible to get the sympathy and

support of the local authorities to the extent necessary for the successful enforcement of the law. We had in New Brunswick a great many years ago an experience of a prohibitory law in advance of public opinion. It was passed by a Government which was either led by the late Sir Leonard Tilley or in which he was a prominent member. It was not a success. It only remained in force one year when it was repealed. I have heard Sir Leonard Tilley himself say nothing could have happened to set back the cause of temperance to a greater extent than the failure to successfully carry out that prohibitory law and the fact of the Government being com- [DOT] pelled to" repeal it. In my own province local option, I think, has been fairly successful. It has produced exceedingly good results and temperance is far and away in advance of what it was 25 or 30 years ago. Great progress has been made. Therefore it is that I am in favour of prohibition by the provinces, aided by Dominion legislation, rather than a general Dominion law. In regard to the Bill itself, a source of discouragement in some of the provinces will be to find that the manufacture of liquor is conducted on a very large scale and that no attempt is made to prohibit it. The temperance people will not be able to understand why it is made illegal to import a gallon of cider into a province where prohibition is in force while you allow whisky to be manufactured on the largest possible scale.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Our Bill does not prohibit the bringing in of a gallon of cider if it is not going to be used for an illegal purpose. As the laws of the provinces stand to-day, roughly speaking, they do not prohibit a man having a gallon of cider in the province, but they do prohibit him selling it. Our law will not prohibit a gallon of cider coming in unless it is going to be sold. There is no provincial law to prevent what is manufactured within the province being sold out of the province, so that whisky and cider will be absolutely on the same footing.

Anybody who has had
experience in prosecuting cases of violation of the liquor laws knows that the liquor will be imported, and has been imported,' ostensibly for private use, but actually for sale and distribution. The difficulty is to prove the real facts so as to enforce the law. The temperance people will be comforted with the fact that where in a province the sale of liquor is prohibited, a gallon of cider could not be imported for sale, and it may be imported ostensibly for private use and yet be disposed of illegally. This Parliament insists on punishing that offence, whereas this .Parliament will enact no statute to rid the province of the evil of manufacturing the strongest kind of intxoi-cating liquors carried on upon a very large scale. That is what will prove disappointing to temperance people. When it is desirable to take steps to put an end to such a condition of affairs we, of course, must leave to the Government to decide. In introducing this Bill my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is beginning just where Parliament began with the Scott Act many years ago. I am afraid that under the Bill in its present form there will have to be gone through the same series of motions in court, the same trials, the same questions, the same appeals, the same proceedings before higher courts that every member of this House as well as every lawyer in the country will remember many years ago when the Canada Temperance Act was first enforced. There is no provision that a conviction by a magistrate shall be final. There is no provision against a writ of certiorari, no provision that there shall not be appeals of all kinds taken. Though you have a provision for the destruction of intoxicating liquors, conviction is not made evidence that the liquor was imported illegally, and in a case of replevin the question must be tried out as to whether the liquor was imported for legal or illegal purposes. Does not the minister think that a conviction, particularly if it should be confirmed, perhaps a conviction without being confirmed, even if the right of appeal were taken away, should be the best evidence that the liquor has been imported illegally and should be subject to forfeiture? Unless that is done, it will have to be tried out as a question entirely separate from the question of the conviction of the individual offender. The minister has also gone to the extent of providing that so far as the taking of criminal proceedings is concerned, the onus oT proving that the liquor was not imported in violation of the law shall be on the defendant, but he has omitted in the Bill any such provision in case the question of the forfeiture of the liquor comes up. Therefore, you might very well have a conviction of the alleged offender by reason of the onus of proof being on him, and by reason of his not being able to satisfy the magistrate, and

you might have a person whose liquor had been forfeited recovering heavy damages against the officers of the law who confiscated the liquor, because in the'case of forfeiture there is no such provision as to the onus of proof. Those are things that perhaps the minister has thought of and does not think desirable to insert in the Bill. If he has not decided adversely in regard to the inclusion of provisions somewhat along the line I have suggested, and which have been found necessary in connection with the enforcement of what is known as the Scott Act, I should like him to give them his consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall certainly welcome any suggestions that will make more assured the effective working of the Bill, but I confess I do not share the apprehensions of the hon. gentleman in so far as the validity of this legislation is concerned. We have been discussing questions that may present some doubt with regard to the extent of powers of manufacturing, but we are not dealing with that at the moment. I have not heard suggested this evening any ground upon which our power to do what we are doing is questioned. I shall certainly welcome any suggestions that would tend to make the working of this Act more effective, and shall of course be prepared to give most careful consideration to any suggestions coming from the hon. gentleman. In so far as the distinction between criminal conviction and what is inserted here, or at all events what was intended to be inserted here, as an additional consequence of the conviction is concerned, possibly it might be an improvement if we had used the words " with respect to which or in regard to which any such conviction has been pronounced," instead of " with respect to which any such offence has been committed." I shall be glad to welcome any assistance that can be given in ensuring that this legislation when enacted shall be effectively enforced. I feel myself that this legislation goes as far as is needed, but the one thing that I am anxious about is^that as far as it does go, it shall be effectively enforced.

What effect will this
Bill have on the wholesale trade? Will a man still be allowed to have a bonded warehouse in a dry province, under the authority of the Inland Revenue Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So long as a province
does not prohibit the possession of liquor
[Mr Pugsley.]
within its limits, I presume it will be possible for a merchant to keep liquor in a bonded warehouse. At all events, this legislation does not affect that question.

It does not touch the
wholesale trade at all?
Mr. DOHERTY': Provinces can deal with the wholesale trade just as well as with the retail trade. I have taken some pains to look into that question, and have not been able to find any suggestion in any of the judgments that the province's power is less with regard to the wholesale trade than it is with regard to the retail trade.
It has generally been assumed that the wholesale trade is. under Trade and Commerce and that the provinces have power to deal with, the retail trade only.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think there is any subject on which more things have been assumed than on this one. I think the confusion on the subject arose in this way: certain provincial legislation did make a distinction between retail and wholesale trade. The Privy Council just took the words of the section and said: "Yes, the province can pass that section." Now, because the section did make a distinction between wholesale and retail trade, the inference seems to have been drawn that because the province did not choose to legislate about wholesale trade, the Privy Council therefore said it could not; whereas the Privy Council was simply answering the question that was put to it. I have looked into this matter, and speak with a certain degree of confidence. It has been assumed, but I think it is a mistaken assumption, that there is a distinction to be made between wholesale and retail trade in liquor from the point of view of the power of the provinces. When it comes to interprovincial trade, there is something to be said about it, and that is what we are trying to take care of; but the fact that a man in selling in large quantities does not affect the power of the province to deal with the question. I do not think that we need in any way be embarrassed by any questions of distinction as regards the quantity in which people deal in liquor.

Under the Inland
Revenue law a merchant is entitled to keep a wholesale shop in any province, where he stores large quantities of liquor which he retails to the public. Will this Act in any way affect that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. I may say that the Privy Council has determined that the fact that a prohibitive provincial law would interfere with the right that a man had in a license from the . Dominion Government would not affect the validity of the provincial law.

I do not wish to disagree with the minister, but lawyers differ in the reading of laws. In the case referred to, did not the Priviy Council say that whilst the province of Ontario would have full power to deal with a license there could be one class of matter falling within section 91, and another class of the same subject falling within section 92?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What I understood to have been decided was this: that the same thing looked at from different standpoints might, according to the standpoint from which it was looked at, be looked upon as purely a local matter within the province, and therefore susceptible of being dealt with by'the province, or as a matter of general or national concern and as such to be dealt with by legislation of this Parliament.
And the moment it dealt with liquor going out of the province the matter fell within the jurisdiction of this Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think there is any doubt that a province cannot legislate about trade outside of itself. I do not think that a province can legislate with regard to the trade that a man is carrying on outside of the province. If I correctly apprehend the state of the jurisprudence our power to make prohibitory enactments about liquor does not rest at all on our powers with regard to the regulation of trade and commerce. It rests upon our power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, and, as was stated in the original case where the matter was decided, is closely linked up with our power to enact criminal la\y. That is what makes our power of prohibition clear. It has clearly been laid down that it is not a matter of regulation of trade and commerce. It might be if you were making regulations as regards foreign trade or if you were making regulations with regard to interprovincial trade, but I think the wisest thing I could do is not to try to define what is included in the regulation of trade and commerce, because the Privy Council has practically said that each thing it has so far been suggested comes under the regulation of trade and commerce, does not do so, and has left us more or less a speculative field as to what is meant by the regulation of trade and commerce. I think, however, it is safe to say, under the decision of the Privy Council, that our right to deal with the traffic in liquor or the use and abuse of liquor does not depend upon our power to deal with the regulation of trade and commerce, and it is probably the safest thing to say that it is a power that we have under our general power to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada.
The power of the provinces to deal with the matter comes, as I understand it4 from their power to deal with all matters of a purely local and private nature within the province. Their lordships have said that a thing that, at the outset or in one set of conditions, may be a purely local matter may come to assume such importance from a Dominion standpoint as to cease to be a purely local matter within the province, although it is always exactly the same thing, and to become a matter of national importance and one calling for action in the interest of the peace, order, and good government of the Dominion. It follows from that that you may have a matter from one point of view within the provincial power and from the other point of view within the Dominion power, and, in effect, this is one of them. There are things that the Privy Council have determined to be susceptible of legislation either by the legislatures looking at it from the provincial point of view, or by the Dominion Parliament looking at it from a national point of view. In such cases they have determined that, where Parliament does legislate, there its legislation is paramount, and the local legislation upon the same subject must give way in the face of existing Dominion legislation. Perhaps the most noteworthy instance is the case where the Canada Temperance Act is brought into force in any district in any province. There it supersedes provincial legislation and the provincial legislation will not be effective. As I understand it, the proposed legislation in Ontario will not affect these counties in Ontario where the Canada Temperance Act is in force, because there the paramount power of Parliament is at work, and ousts from the field the power from a local point of view of the province.

The minister perhaps has not noticed that the party who drafted this

Bill, although he appears to have attempted to follow the Act that was passed in 1908, has not altogether done so. This matter is nothing new; this Act has been on the Statute Book for a number of years, excepting that it- applied to counties in which the Scott Act had been adopted. We are now attempting to apply it to parts of Canada where some other Act in addtion to the Scott Act has been adopted. This legislation has been on the Statute Book since 1908, and in looking over the Act that was passed in 1908, I am inclined to think that some language that ought to have been inserted in this Bill has been left out, and I would like to draw the attention of the , minister to that, so that perhaps his Bill might be amended. The Act of 1908 was an amendment to the Scott Act. Section 117 says:
From the day on which this part comes into force and takes effect in any county or city, and for so long thereafter as, and while the same continues or is in force therein, no person shall, except as in this part specially provided by himself, his clerk, servant, or agent,-
(a)	expose or keep for sale, within such county or city, any intoxicating liquor; or,
(b)	directly or indirectly on any pretense or upon any device, within any such county or city, sell or barter, or, in consideration of the purchase of any other property, give to any other person any intoxicating liquor; or,
(c)	send, ship, bring or carry or cause to be sent, shipped, brought, or carried to or into any such county or & city, any intoxicating liquor; or,
(d)	deliver to any consignee or other person, or store, warehouse, or keep for delivery, any intoxicating liquor so sent, shipped, brought or carried.
The Bill that we are now considering has these words in the first section:
Any person who by himself, his clerk, servant or agent, shall send, ship, take, bring or carry,
But the words
or cause to be sent, shipped, brought or carried.
are omitted. I think those words are important, because it is so easy to evade this kind of legislation. A merchant in a wholesale district that is shipping into a dry province might cause some other person to send the liquor for him, and in that case he would not be liable at all because he did not do it himself. The purpose of putting that language into the Act was to prevent that. I think that subsection d ought to be added to the Bill:
Deliver to any consignee or other person, or store, warehouse, or keep for delivery, any intoxicating liquor so sent, shipped, brought or carried.

I would suggest to the minister to look into that and see if his Bill would not be improved by the addition of that subsection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall 'be glad to look into the matter and see what is best to be done. At first glance I would' think-qui faoit per alium tacit per se-the man who causes to be sent, shipped, brought or carried, must send or ship the liquor through his clerk, servant or agent at the very least. If I cause a man to carry, then that man is my agent for the purpose of carrying. I am, however, willing to give the matter thought, and if it is possible that adding those words will add any force to the Bill, I shall 'be glad to insert them.
This question has all been threshed out in the courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Subsection d is a
substantive prohibitory law. We are not purporting to make such a law; we are purporting to assure the effectiveness of the provincial laws that may be made. As regards the warehousing and storing, all that will happen in the province into which the liquor has been sent, and once it is in there the province will do the legislating about what quantity of liquor people can store and hold, and so on, under its law. / What we are undertaking to do is to prevent the liquor being sent in for the purpose of violation. A province can take ample care of the violations of its own law that happen within its own limits. This Bill is trying to prevent violations within the limits of a province which are brought about by the action of people outside. The Canadian Temperance Act was making >a substantive prohibitory law prohibiting certain things and that section was inserted to protect those districts that adopted the Canadian Temperance Act from the action of people outside of those districts. That was to protect the temperance district under the Canada Temperance Act from tlhe action, detrimental to the carrying out of that Act within the borders of the district, of peoeple outside the district. Our legislation is to protect the enforcement of the provtineial law within the ''province against interference by the action of outside people. [DOT] We are not making prohibition of a particular thing; the province will do the prohibiting and will attend to the man who warehouses or keeps in store liquor within

the province. With regard to the suggestion that we should have the words "or cause," etc., I will give it consideration. I think it fair to assume that the persons who'drafted the Canada Temperance Act knew that there was a difference between the two things, and I do not mean to say that there was not. If there is a difference, we want to get at the man who, in any shape, is a party to the getting of liquor into a province for the known purpose of its being used to violate the law of the province.
Mr. LEMIiEUX: I would like to speak rather as a layman than as a lawyer upon this matter. I voted for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Calgary [DOT](Mr. Bennett), and for this reason: I am in favour of temperance, but I am against a measure of Dominion-wide prohibition, until it is backed up by public opinion in each of the several provinces. But, while I voted for this general purpose, I wish it to be understood that it is because I respect provincial Tights and public opinion in this matter within the various provinces. But the mo.ment a province has declared itself for prohibition-and I take it, as a resident of this province of Ontario, that this province is overwhelmingly in favour of total prohibition-I stand by the province in that movement. But, if I appose Dominion-wide prohibition, as moved the other day by my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), I want it to be perfectly understood that it is my opinion that this Government 'should, by the present legislation, give effect to that provincial prohibition in a satisfactory way. And how can you make your Bill effective, if it does not go further than the present measure? I understand that when a province is declared to be " dry, " not only will the province expect that there will be no license given for the retail trade, but that this Parliament, by its legislation, will prevent the wholesaling of liquor to go on in that province. My bon. friend (Mr. Doherty) shakes his head. But if that is not provided for in your legislation you will have no prohibition in Ontario, and you will not meet public opinion by your legislation. My hon. friend stated that he understood that the province had the right to restrict the wholesale liquor trade as much as the retail. As to that, I believe there is a strong doubt. I am not prepared to cite authorities, and havie not the judgment of the Privy Courieil on this question before
me. But I know that my hon. friend is sincere in that-he has been associated for years with the cause of temperance in his own province. But he knows perfectly well that if you do not prohibit the wholesale as well as the retail trade you have no prohibition in the province, and you run counter to public opinion in that province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, if I had any doubt that the wholesale trade coulc^ not be prohibited I would give consideration to the matter. But with all the respect I have for the hon. gentleman's opinion, I have not any doubt that the wholesale trade can be dealt with as effectually as the retail trade. I am dealing now with buying and, selling.
Do not the wholesalers get their licenses from the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know that in the province of Quebec they issue a wholesale liquor license, and a retail liquor license. The license that comes from the Dominion, as I understand it, is the inland revenue license for the manufacture. As to the manufacture, I am not prepared to speak so positively.
I did not mean tc refer to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then I misapprehend
the hon. gentleman's statement. He spoke of the wholesale trade as contrasted with the retail trade. If it is a question of manufacture, then, to come back to what I said at the outset, we are endeavouring to deal with this thing for the provinces of Canada. Each province can legislate to protect itself against the free use or consumption of liquor, and we are prepared to supplement it to the extent of the suggested amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver, namely, that if any man who manufactures in a province abuses the fact of his being there, so as to violate the provincial law, it is suggested-and, as at present advised, I expect to be prepared to accept that suggestion-that we should withdraw the inland revenue license, which will end his manufacture. The provincial law will protect the people of the province, and all that would be left would be the manufacture for export purposes exclusively1. If a man is manufacturing whisky, let us say, in Ontario-and let us assume for a moment that Quebec is a non-prohibitory province and Ontario is a prohibitory province-what injury will be done the province of Ontario because

whisky is being manufactured within that province and goes into the province of Quebec for consumption there? Or, to carry it a step further, if we assume that all the provinces have declared that they do not want liquor sold within their borders, what injury can come to any province or to the Dominion, if within one of the provinces liquor is manufactured exclusively for export and goes to people outside who do not take the same view of * this subject that we dp? With this suggested amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver, it does seem to me that we come to the assistance of the provinces in creating a situation where the manufacturer	who Will	not	see to it
that his distilling infringes no provincial law, shall have	no license.
That would be an end of his business. That would he a prohibition of the manufacture upon any man who does not absolutely conform to the provincial law. If I am right in the view that the importation for unlawful purpose being guarded against the manufacture being carried on in the province, does not injure the people of the province if they are locally protected against it, we should pause and consider what is the evil to-day within Canada that would be remedied by the entire suppression of the manufacture of liquor even for export.

I would ask the minister if this principle that he is enunciating is this: so long as we are not injured, we do not care a rap about the people outside? If the province, therefore, not caring about other people and being willing to take the revenue or whatever direct or indirect benefit may arise from the manufacture of liquor, does not see fit to prohibit the manufacture of it, there is no reason why the Dominion Government should prohibit. We might as well have whatever money there is in it as long as we are not injured by the consumption of it. That seems to be the stand of the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are quite willing
to let other people be the judges of what injures them. That, I think, is the better way of putting it. We rather like to think ourselves competent to be the judges of what injures us. Say that the people in South America think that whisky is good for them. Is there any duty upon this Parliament to legislate to protect the people of South America from what they think is good for them? Of course, we may have such a conviction of the intrinsic -evil of this as
to press upon ourselves that in a great humanitarian cause we ought to legislate for the protection of the outside world.

Under this Bill as proposed, it would be legal, would it not, for a distillery in Ontario to sell to a wholesale dealer in Ontario who would tell the distiller that he intended to export the liquor to some province where a prohibitory law was not in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not if the province of
Ontario chose tb legislate that it would not be. We will not give Ontario or anyone else any more prohibition than they give themselves. Let us say that Ontario prohibits the distiller and every one else from selling liquor for consumption in Ontario; then our Bill will not help them, because they do not need any help. They have authority over the sale by that distiller within the province.
And over the manufacture too?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not prepared to
say that they have authority to prohibit the manufacture if the manufacture is being carried on in such manner as not to constitute its consequences a local evil within the province. Although their lordships were careful not to give us any definition of what they had in view, I should suppose that probably the manufacture absolutely and exclusively for export could not come under that definition.

Suppose	it were done
in this way. The wholesale men in Ontario have their retail customers in various provinces in the Dominion. Could the provincial legislature prohibit the distillers from appointing these wholesale men as their agents for the purpose of export? If the local legislatures cannot do that and this Parliament will not prevent its being done, the distillers through their wholesale agents could distribute the liquor all through Ontario and so defeat the prohibitory law of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Any one, whether he is a manufacturer or not, can manage to sell whisky in violation of the law of Ontario. Tim distiller will be like every one else when he is selling his whisky in Ontario, if Ontario prohibits his selling it he will be violating the law.

Suppose he appoints
the wholesale dealer his agent, ostensibly for export, and the liquor is sent to the warehouses of the wholesale dealers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The wholesale dealer proceeds to violate the law by selling in Ontario.

That is what the temperance people want to stop if they can.
Mr. DOHE^tTY: They have their law, and they will punish that man if he violates it. Shall we punish people for violation of provincial laws within the limits of the province? Surely the provinces can take care of that as well as we can, and just as effectively.

My hon. friend knows that this legislation which he introduced to-day was framed-and it was so heralded -with the view of standing behind those provinces which adopted prohibition. There is a big movement to-day in Canada in favour of prohibition. It is one of the spiritual sides of the present war; the people -I will not say in every province, but generally speaking-are in favour of prohibition. The Government says: Until it is conceded that this is the general feeling throughout Canada in all the provinces, we will leave this matter to the provinces themselves. Can any one deny that at least two and perhaps three provinces are to-day wedded to total prohibition?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Why do they not pass it?
The province of Ontario, of which I am a resident, is to-day strongly and overwhelmingly in favour of total prohibition.
No, that is not correct.

Whilst I was not ready the other evening to stand by the motion of the member for Vancouver, because I am not convinced that in all provinces the sentiment is unanimous, yet my temperance principles will impel me to stand by any province which adopts prohibition for itself: I understood that my hon. friend would come here with legislation that would make good that prohibition in the particular province. I know that my hon. friend would not resort to quibbling; he has too great a reputation for that. But he knows that his legislation will not be backed by public opinion in the province of Ontario if it does not go further. If you do not prevent the distillation of whisky and strong beverages in the province of Ontario, you are not meeting public opinion as expressed in this province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Have they every expressed it?

The minister knows-I can appeal to any member from the province of Ontario here this evening-that public opinion in this province has been overwhelmingly expressed of late in favour of a measure of total prohibition.
I deny that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When Ontario shall have passed a measure of total prohibition -let us understand the word-it will have a measure of total prohibition, because we will keep the liquor from coming into the province from outside; and if the province of Ontario wants to. say there shall be no liquor in Ontario-let us not talk about manufacture-they have a right to say so.
(Mr. LEMIEUX: I am glad to take my hon. friend at his word-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is my view of it.

But now let us put a concrete case. If to-morrow the Legislature of Ontario declares that it is the wish and the desire of the .province, speaking through its representatives, to have total prohibition, and that it is necessary to have legislation from the Dominion Parliament in order to make effective that total prohibition, do I understand my hon. friend to say that he will give the province of Ontario the measure of relief it will ask?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Ontario will not need the slightest measure of relief when she gets her mind made up to get total prohibition. If she chooses to consider that for the abatement of the evil, as a local evil, the essential thing is that there shall be no liquor in Ontario, let her say so by her Legislature, and that will be, in my opinion, .a good law and an effective law, and she will not need any assistance from this Dominion.
Does the minister say that the Provincial Legislature can say that there will be no liquor manufactured in Ontario for export?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe she can say there shall be no liquor in Ontario.

For export?
iMr. DOHERTY: If she wants to go on and add these words she may put doubt upon it, but she can say there shall be no liquor in Ontario, and then there will be no right for any man to have liquor in Ontario.

I thought some time ago that I understood this Bill. It seemed to me to he very simple and very readily understandable. , But I am not sure, after the Bill has oome under the dissecting knives of lawyers on both sides of the House, that I am not in the same position as the man who undertook to eat a very tough piece of beefsteak, and who, although he was a very strong man, after he had completed the act of mastication, was too weak to swallow the beef-it had taken all his strength to masticate it. It seems to me that if the province of Ontario wants to prevent or prohibit the use of intoxicating liquors as a beverage within the province of Ontario two Acts are necessary. One of these Acts lies entirely within the power of the Provincial Legislature, and the other within the power of this Parliament. What are those two necessary Acts? The Provincial Government can pass an. Act prohibiting the sale by any person or persons within the province of Ontario of intoxicating liquors for beverage purposes to any other person or persons. That includes not only the man in the retail, but in the wholesale trade, and the distiller and brewer as well. That is to say, Ontario can say to any man in the province of Ontario, no matter whether he be in the retail trade, or a private citizen, or a man in the wholesale trade, or a distiller, or a brewer, you shall not sell liquor for beverage purposes to any person in Ontario. But that is not enough, and in order to make prohibition effective what more is needed? While that Act would apply to every person in the province, it would not apply to persons outside, and the difficulty of prohibiting or preventing the sale for beverage purposes in Ontario rests upon the fact that some person in Quebec or Manitoba may send liquor into Ontario. This Act, as I understand it, steps in and says: You in the province of Ontario say you do not want any person to sell liquor to any person else in that province; you can pass laws affecting people inside of your own bounds, making it an offence for any person, brewer, distiller, wholesaler or retailer to sell to any one else within the province. That is as far as you can go. Then this Act steps in and says: We will do that act which is necessary to make your Act effective, we will prevent any person in Quebec or Manitoba or any other province sending any liquor into the province of Ontario for beverage purposes. There you have your prohibition. Suppose you start in Ontario to get Dominion-wide pro-
hibition? Take the case of Hiram Walker, one of the distillers in Ontario. Ontario passes a prohibitory Act and by it tells Hiram Walker that he must not sell liquor to any person in Ontario for beverage purposes, and the province can make the fine as high as they want to. Quebec comes along and passes a prohibitory law, and then Hiram is shut out of Quebec. Manitoba comes along and passes a similar law, and Hiram is shut out of Manitoba. So each province could shut Hiram out from sending his liquor into that province. What does that amount to? Then after each province goes as far as it wants to in preventing the use of liquor for beverage purposes within its bounds, the firm of Walker or any other distiller is in this position, that they cannot sell their liquor to any person within the province of Ontario where their works are, or to any person within any other province that has passed a prohibitory law. Of course a prohibitory law would apply to all Canada if each province passed such a law. But the distiller can still run his manufacturing establishment and sell liquor to the United States or to England or to the Argentine Republic or any other part of the world. I entirely agree-and I feel it is worth while to express my pleasure at being able to agree with the hon. member for St. John in some things-in the hon. member's expression of approval of the local option law. I also agree in the opinion expressed by him that there should be a strong public sentiment behind any prohibitory law. I entirely agree with that. I want to say that no person who believes in local option can disbelieve in the right, of the province to handle this matter as a province, and that no person who believes in provincial autonomy, in the provinces passing or not passing prohibitory laws, can conscientiously advocate that this Parliament should pass a law to prohibit the manufacture and importation of intoxicating liquors. I say that no person who believes in each province having a local prohibitory law for itself, if it chooses, can conscientiously ask that this Parliament should pass a law to prohibit the manufacture and importation of intoxicating liquor, because the moment this Parliament passes an Act to prohibit the manufacture and importation of liquors that moment this Parliament overrides the opinion, perhaps, of British Columbia or of Quebec. We will assume that Quebec says: We are not prepared to pass a prohibitory law, that the

sentiment in the province is not sufficiently strong to warrant it. Hon. gentlemen would not argue that it would be wise on the part of this Parliament to pass an Act which would enforce on that province, contrary to the sentiment of the majority of the people of that province, an Act which must necessarily be ineffective and inoperative because there would not be sufficient sentiment behind it. I think I have stated the effect of the Act fairly, and I believe that it all comes, as I said before, to those two points. If a province passes a prohibitory law-and it can pass a prohibitory law that applies to a distiller or a brewer just the same as it applies to a private ciizen,-it can prohibit selling to any person within the province but it cannot prohibit a person in the province of Quebec from selling to a person in the province of Ontario. But this Act steps in and does that very thing which it is necessary to do to make the Act effective within the limits of whatever province sees fit to pass prohibitory legislation.

Cannot you more
effectively prohibit the sale by the distillery by wiping out the distillery itself?

No, I do not think so. I do not think that would be fair to the other provinces. Let us suppose that in one province there was a sentiment of 75 per cent against prohibition; will my hon. friend say that in such a province a prohibitory law could be made effective? I am of the opinion that you want a strong public sentiment behind a prohibition law or any other kind of sumptuary law. I also believe that if you pass a law, such as a sumptuary law, against public sentiment, and that law proves to be ineffective, you have done harm to the cause you want to benefit, because you have made the law a farce. But if the sentiment in the province of Quebec is strong for prohibition Quebec will pass a prohibitory law. The same is true of all the provinces, and that being so, of what earthly use would it be for the distilleries to continue their business? If their sales were confined to the Dominion of Canada, and if each of the provinces passes a prohibitory law, they would automatically go out of business. After each of the provinces has passed a prohibition measure it will be time enough for this Parliament to consider the closing down of the distilleries and breweries, even those that are selling to outside countries. 1 do not think it would be wise legislation
on the part of this Parliament to undertake to do'that at the present time while opinion is being formed in the various provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is pretty nearly twelve o'clock, there is another day after this .and we have had a pretty extended preliminary canter. Is the committee prepared to pass this clause and rise and report progress?

My hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) is very desirous that he should 'be allowed to speak on this first section. The Minister of Justice intimated that he would go on as far as possible. I do not see much object in passing the clause because it may be that upon consideration some amendment will he suggested to it. The Minister of Justice himself intimated that he might amend that clause. Perhaps we had better rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is one amendment that I would -be disposed to suggest to the first clause and that would be to provide a maximum as well as a minimum penalty. Amended in that way, I would be glad if the clause were passed. I do not think it need interfere with anybody's liberty of discussion and we could truthfully report that we had made some progress.
Progress reported.
